inline.s: (18) The mark of full armpits. The hollows beneath the two armpits are filled out. (They are not concave.)
(19) The mark of a body like a lion. This means that the deportment is grave and majestic.
(20) The mark of a body upright and straight. The bodily form is well proportioned, without stooping or bending.

(21) The mark of rounded and full shoulders. This means that the whole form of the two shoulders is neither raised nor sloping, but round, thick, and full. It differs from the even fullness of the seven places above.
(22) The mark of forty teeth. All forty teeth are complete. (An ordinary person has at most thirty-six teeth.)
(23) The mark of teeth white, even, and closely set. All forty teeth are white and pure, even and regular, firm and closely set.
(24) The mark of the four teeth white and pure. The four great teeth are of the purest and brightest white.
(25) The mark of the jaws like a lion's. The two cheeks are full and prominent, like a lion's cheeks.
(26) The mark of obtaining the supreme flavor. There is saliva in the throat; whatever food is eaten, it all becomes a flavor beyond compare.
(27) The mark of the broad and long tongue. The tongue is broad and long, soft, red, and thin. Spread out, it is broad enough to cover the face, and long enough to reach the hairline.
(28) The mark of the Brahma voice, deep and far-reaching. Brahma means purity. The sound of the voice is pure: nearby one does not find it loud, yet in the distance it is also heard.
(29) The mark of the eyes deep blue in color. The color of the pupils is like deep blue, utterly pure and luminous, like refined gold.
(30) The mark of eyelashes like a bull king's. The eyelashes are distinct, sparse, and supremely fine, like those of a bull king.
(31) The mark of the white hair between the eyebrows. Between the two brows there is a hair, white and pure, soft and curling, turning to the right and emitting light.
(32) The mark of the fleshy topknot. On the crown of the head there is flesh that rises up like a topknot.

These thirty-two marks are also called the marks of a great man, also called the marks of a great being, and also called the marks adorned by a hundred merits, meaning that a hundred kinds of merit and virtue adorn a single mark. To perfect all thirty-two requires passing through a hundred great kalpas; hence it is said, "a hundred kalpas of cultivating the marks and excellences." Merit and virtue are precisely the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra. Therefore the Chapter on Conduct and Vows says: "This good man well obtains a human body. Perfecting all the merit and virtue of Samantabhadra, before long he will be like the bodhisattva Samantabhadra, and will quickly accomplish a wondrous form-body complete with the thirty-two marks of a great man." One should know that the marks and excellences are all accomplished by great compassion and great vows. Why cultivate these marks and excellences? Because all sentient beings without exception cling to marks. If they see the marks and excellences, they then give rise to a joyful mind and a reverent mind. Only then are they willing to hear the Dharma, and only then can they give rise to faith. Moreover, Brahma kings, Indra, and wheel-turning kings also possess these marks, and bodhisattvas too often have them; but because the excellences are not complete, they are not equal to a Buddha. As for "marks and excellences," this does not mean that the marks are extremely fine. Rather, the great marks are called marks, and the subtle marks are called excellences. And "great" and "subtle" do not refer to size either. The great marks are seen as soon as they meet the eye. The subtle marks require careful observation before their excellence is known. The subtle marks are precisely what adorns the great marks. Thus the Buddha has thirty-two marks and accordingly eighty excellences, also called the eighty minor marks that follow the form; "following the form" means that they follow the thirty-two marks of form. Bodhisattvas, though they too have excellences, do not come up to the Buddha's completeness. The eighty are: (1) an invisible crown of the head; (2) nostrils that do not show; (3) brows like the new moon; (4) earlobes that hang down; (5) a body firm and solid as Nārāyaṇa; (6) bones like linked hooks; (7) the body turning at once like an elephant king; (8) when walking, the feet leaving the ground four inches, yet with imprint patterns; (9) nails of the color of red copper, thin and glossy; (10) knee-bones firm and round; and so on up to (80) hands and feet all displaying marks of virtue. Fearing prolixity, I do not give them in full; see the Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahayana for details. As for the names of the thirty-two marks, they are stated according to the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom; other books may differ. The thirty-two marks and eighty excellences above are what the transformation body manifests. As for the Buddha's reward body, it has more than this number; for the body has eighty-four thousand, even immeasurable, marks and excellences.

These two sections, on the great chiliocosm and on the thirty-two marks, if viewed together, hold inexhaustible wondrous meaning. For on these two matters our World-Honored One says "not so" and "is called," which is most intimate and flavorful. If those who hear the Dharma can truly ponder them with wholehearted attention, they may become utterly clear and luminous regarding the essential purport of prajñā. To sum up, this can be divided into four sections to make its meaning clear: first, clarifying by way of sentient beings; second, clarifying by way of cause and effect; third, clarifying by way of emptiness and existence being simultaneously and together present; fourth, clarifying by way of the ultimate definitive meaning.

First, clarifying by way of sentient beings. In other words, the reason the World-Honored One says "not so" and "is called" concerning these two matters, the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks, is that he is giving intimate guidance on the side of sentient beings. How is this so? The world is the environment on which all sentient beings depend. Without a world, how could they settle body and establish life? And if the Tathagata did not manifest the marks of the thirty-two response bodies, from where would all sentient beings hear the Dharma? From where would they give rise to faith? Speaking thus, these two matters are, on the side of sentient beings, of the most vital concern, as can be known. Therefore, speaking in terms of nature, although fundamentally they are all provisional names for what is condition-arisen and illusory, still to call them provisional names is acceptable, while to call them "not so" is greatly unacceptable. Hence it is said "is called," making clear that although they are provisional names, they are truly so, and thus cannot be destroyed. Yet one should know that the world is ultimately a field of dust; if all sentient beings grasp and cling to these dust-marks, the mind is not pure. When the mind is impure, the land is impure; how then can they end birth and death and escape rebirth? Further, one should know that the Buddha's response body is a form manifested by the Tathagata of the dharma-body. That is, only one who has realized the dharma-body can manifest the response body. Why manifest a response body? Without manifesting these marks, sentient beings would have no way to hear the Dharma. And the Tathagata manifests the response body to speak the Dharma originally because he wishes all sentient beings to realize the dharma-body they inherently possess. If sentient beings grasp and cling to the marks of this response body, they will be unable to see the nature. Why? Because if they cannot reflect back upon their own nature, then even standing face to face before a Buddha of thirty-two marks, they still cannot see the Tathagata. Would this not greatly contradict the Buddha's original purpose in manifesting the thirty-two marks? Therefore in every case he says "not so," making clear that in terms of marks it is indeed so, but in terms of nature it is not so, and hence one should not cling. Such guidance is intimacy itself.

Second, clarifying by way of cause and effect. In other words, the World-Honored One's establishing this teaching on these two matters is intended to enable sentient beings to understand clearly the true meaning of cause and effect. How is this so? Whence comes this dusty, ordinary great chiliocosm? It is what sentient beings feel in common through their shared karma. Whence come these supremely wondrous thirty-two marks? They are what the World-Honored One accomplished through perfuming and cultivation over many kalpas. That being so, both of these are nothing but the law of cause and effect, as can be clearly known. Cause and effect means arising through the meeting of conditions. Because they are condition-arisen, they are illusory existents; because they are illusory existents, they are provisional names. Yet although they are provisional names, where there is a cause there must be an effect, which is never destroyed; hence it is said "is called." The words "is called" are used to make sentient beings deeply reverence cause and effect: though empty in nature, the marks exist, and not the slightest bit is off or can be escaped. If one knows that cause and effect are empty in nature, existing in marks, and inescapable, one should then cultivate the supreme pure cause that is neither marked nor unmarked, in order to realize the supreme wondrous fruit that is neither marked nor unmarked. What is meant by "neither marked nor unmarked"? It is to understand that dharmas arising from causes and conditions are precisely empty and precisely provisional, precisely provisional and precisely empty, and that one does not cling to either extreme, thereby according with the supreme meaning of the middle way. One should know that "neither marked nor unmarked" and "the supreme meaning of the middle way" are the true reality of the nature, which is so from the beginning. Therefore to cultivate and uphold in this way is precisely prajñā-pāramitā. That is why cultivating this supreme cause must win the supreme fruit. Hence concerning the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks he says in every case "not so." He says "not so" in every case so that sentient beings may neither destroy the marks of cause and effect nor fail to return and merge into the nature. This is to be free of clinging to both emptiness and existence, and to accord with the middle way.

Third, clarifying by way of emptiness and existence being simultaneously and together present. This makes clear that the World-Honored One's establishing this teaching is so that, by hearing this Dharma, beings may understand clearly the reason why emptiness and existence are simultaneously and together present. How is this so? The single word "not" is spoken to keep one from clinging to existence. The single word "is" is spoken to keep one from clinging to emptiness. And to say both "not" and "is," speaking the two together, is to keep one from clinging to either extreme. Why may one cling to neither? Because inwardly this body and outwardly the world, the two rewards of dependent and proper, are none of them anything but what arises from the union of causes and conditions. At the time conditions meet and it arises, the names and marks of the two rewards, dependent and proper, plainly appear: how could one cling to emptiness? At the time conditions disperse and it ceases, where is this body, where is this world: how could one cling to existence? Nor is this all. As for the two rewards, dependent and proper, when the time of their condition-arising comes, since it is a union of causes and conditions, we call it arising. From this one can see that apart from causes and conditions there is no other real dharma. Therefore when the provisional name appears, that is precisely the time of non-existence. Hence it is said, "existence is precisely non-existence." And again, when it is the time of non-existence, that is precisely the time the provisional name appears. Hence it is said, "non-existent yet existing." Viewed together, is this not emptiness and existence being simultaneously and together present? Since they are simultaneously and together present, clinging to either emptiness or existence is wrong. Therefore the present joint statement of "not" and "is" is precisely to enable those who hear the Dharma to understand the meaning that emptiness and existence are together present and neither may be clung to. Moreover, the two rewards, dependent and proper, are matters of name and mark so evident that all beings see them in common. Since these are simultaneously empty and existent, the rest can be understood at a glance. And since they are the matters most intimately and vitally connected with sentient beings, and here emptiness and existence alike may not be clung to, the rest can be understood clearly. In the two sections above, which are free of names, words, and speech, only the side of existence was being dismissed. In these two sections, both sides, emptiness and existence, are dismissed; this is the utmost in cutting off deluded thoughts.

Fourth, clarifying by way of the ultimate meaning. This explains that the World-Honored One speaks these two sections in order to enable sentient beings to comprehend thoroughly the nature-body in which the path of words is cut off and the reach of the mind is extinguished. How is this so? Since the two rewards, dependent and proper, are both condition-arisen, one can know that they are merely marks of the coming together of causes and conditions. Therefore in the sutra they are called "is called." "Is called" makes clear that they are provisionally named as arising. Since they are provisionally named as arising, one can see that in truth they have never arisen. Therefore in the sutra he says of them "not so." "Not so" makes clear that they are fundamentally unborn. Since there is no such thing as arising, there is also no such thing as ceasing. That being so, all dharmas are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing; but ordinary beings do not know this, and in their delusion take them to be truly arising and ceasing, and following upon that, deluded thoughts arise in confusion. Therefore the World-Honored One calls them pitiable.

One should further know that body, mind, and world are fundamentally without arising and ceasing; yet marks of arising and ceasing are seen, and names of arising and ceasing are established. There is no other reason: it is truly the empty illusion of deluded, pitiable ordinary beings, the false marks conjured by deluded thoughts, and the names and words forcibly established by deluded thoughts. When the sutra says "is called," it is exactly so. This is the ultimate definitive meaning of "is called." Therefore if one is apart from thought, then the names and words of body, mind, and world do not even remain: how much less the names of arising and ceasing, and how much less could arising and ceasing be spoken of. In this way all marks are extinguished and one enters the true reality-body. Why? The nature-body of true suchness has from the very beginning been equal and thus. It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent. It extends even to being neither all dharmas nor not all dharmas. In sum, as soon as thought arises, it is not so; and even the "not so" of the arising of thought is also not so. This is what is meant by being apart from the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations. When the sutra says "then it is not," it is exactly so. This is the ultimate definitive meaning of "then it is not."

This ultimate definitive meaning is present wherever the text above says "then it is not" or "is called." Yet it was not spoken of earlier, and is spoken only now, for there is deep purpose in this. The text below says "deeply understood the meaning and purport," from which one can know that by this point in the sutra the deep meaning should be made clear. Hence the matter was temporarily set aside above. This is what is meant by leading from the shallow into the deep, drawing people into what is wondrous. Further, this meaning is most conveniently stated with regard to body, mind, and world. And again, in this request for the name and the upholding, the sutra's meaning is precisely to make clear the cutting off of thought as a means of realizing the nature. If one wishes to cut off thought and realize the nature, one cannot do so without upholding the ultimate definitive meaning. Hence it is said that by this point in the sutra the deep meaning should be made clear. Knowing this, one knows that this meaning should only be brought out here. To move it earlier would be too soon; to move it later would be too late. In expounding the sutras and speaking the Dharma, one must let the text and meaning be without error. For meanings have shallow and deep, and the text has its proper sequence. If one does not speak when one should speak, and speaks when one should not, this is an error in the text. Even if the meaning is without error, it is still idle talk and carries fault. This is a point that anyone with the vow to propagate the Dharma must not fail to know.

Further, above, when he says "then it is not," he only says "then it is not"; when he says "is called," he only says "is called." But the meaning of the fourth layer is not so. When he says "is called," the intent of "then it is not" is included; and when he says "then it is not," the intent of "is called" is also included. This too is the ultimate definitive meaning. How could it be that only dismissing marks and speaking of the nature counts as the ultimate definitive meaning? One should know that if there were only negation and no illumination, only extinction and nothing preserved, then what was spoken would not be the ultimate definitive meaning. Within negation there is illumination; within extinction there is preservation: only this is the ultimate definitive meaning. For without negation and extinction one cannot see the nature; yet a rigid negation and a rigid extinction also cannot see the nature. Hearing this ultimate definitive meaning, one should ponder it with wholehearted attention. A difference of a hairsbreadth becomes an error of a thousand miles. This is of the utmost importance.

Now let these two sections on not destroying provisional names and the two sections above on returning and merging into the nature-body be viewed together: there is a further essential meaning that must urgently be made clear. One should know that the reason for first causing detachment by way of the names and words of prajñā, and then causing non-clinging by way of the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks, is nothing else. It is because the nature-body is absolutely unconditioned. The moment one falls into names and language, there is the namer and the named, the speaker and the spoken. Since there is a subject and an object, they plainly become a pair of opposites. Where there is the slightest mark of opposition, it is no longer the absolute body. The Buddha speaks prajñā to enable people to see the nature. For prajñā-pāramitā originally arises from the principle-body of true suchness and right wisdom. Therefore by this he causes detachment from names and words, making clear the meaning that one who would realize the nature must dismiss marks. And further, because this body is absolutely unconditioned, it can merge and absorb all worldly and world-transcending dharmas. As the Awakening of Faith says, "Because the Tathagata-garbha is complete with immeasurable intrinsic merit and virtue" (this sentence makes clear the greatness of marks), "because it can produce all worldly and world-transcending causes and effects" (this sentence makes clear the greatness of function). From this one sees that marks and function cannot be apart from the body. That is, because the body is great, the marks and function it absorbs are also great. Now these two sections on not destroying provisional names, in speaking of the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks, precisely make clear the greatness of marks. For they are all manifested by the nature-body: the so-called immeasurable intrinsic merit and virtue. Further, the great chiliocosm is what sentient beings feel in common through their shared karma, and is the cause and effect of worldly dharmas. The thirty-two marks are what the Buddha accomplished through perfuming and cultivation over many kalpas, and are the cause and effect of world-transcending dharmas. From this one sees that these two also make clear, in passing, the greatness of function. Moreover, to bring up the great chiliocosm is to absorb all cause and effect of worldly dharmas; to bring up the Buddha's thirty-two marks is to absorb all cause and effect of world-transcending dharmas. Further, to speak of the world is to absorb all vast marks; to speak of atoms is to absorb all subtle marks. That being so, if one here makes clear non-clinging, then one should not cling to anything at all, as can be known. If one here makes clear non-destruction, then one should not destroy anything at all, as can also be understood. Why should one not cling to anything? Because marks and function should merge into the nature-body. Why should one not destroy anything? Because the body must be complete with marks and function.

Moreover, from the sequence of first speaking of returning and merging into the nature-body and afterwards speaking of not destroying provisional names, it is plainly shown to students that at the outset they should use the work of sweeping away in order to remove the stains of old habituations, so that this mind may gradually become pure and there is hope of seeing the nature. Even the marks of names and words must still be swept away; then one can know that not the slightest mark may remain in the mind. Why? Because the nature is fundamentally not marks. Yet if one uses only this work, one must guard against falling into one-sided emptiness. Therefore one should also be all-embracing. All-embracing means that nature and marks are perfectly fused, unobstructed and free. Hence the teaching that follows on not destroying provisional names. This is to make clear the meaning of perfect fusion without obstruction. For the reason he first speaks of "not" before speaking of "is called" is to make clear that illusory existence does not depart from true emptiness, and that marks, being not the nature, are not fused. Therefore although one does not destroy marks, one must also not cling to marks, and only then can there be perfect fusion without obstruction. Without obstruction means that marks do not obstruct the nature. Further, the reason he speaks both of "not" and then of "is called" is to make clear that true emptiness does not hinder illusory existence, and that the nature, being not marks, would not be revealed. Therefore although one does not cling to marks, one should also not destroy marks, and only then is there non-obstruction and perfect fusion. Perfect fusion means that the nature does not reject marks. Such is the meaning here, the most refined and essential meaning of these four sections. The essential purport of prajñā-pāramitā is thoroughly laid bare. This is precisely the reason why the Diamond Prajñā-pāramitā is to be upheld. If one does not understand this, then with regard to the sutra's meaning, even if one happens to speak a thing or two, it will never touch the vital spot. Then what is called understanding is not true understanding. Since it is not true understanding, how can one uphold it? Then what is called practice is in truth blind practice. In this way, though one studies Buddhism diligently and laboriously, one can never gain great benefit, and may even walk into a side path without knowing it. The opposite is to advance a thousand miles a day and gain inexhaustible benefit. Prajñā is the fundamental meaning within the Buddhadharma, and is also the ultimate definitive meaning. If a student of Buddhism is unclear about this fundamental and ultimate meaning, he is forever seeking among branches and leaves. Having not seen the Way, how can he speak of cultivating the Way? Hence he cannot gain benefit. The old theory that the three teachings share one source is nothing but drawing analogies and forcing connections among the branches and leaves of the Buddhadharma. As for the fundamental and ultimate meaning, there is no way to compare it at all. One should know that the Buddhadharma surpasses all else precisely in this. If one studies Buddhism without understanding this meaning, one remains outside the gate. Hence it is said above: "All Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra." This plainly shows that the Buddhadharma must be entered through this gate.

Confucians have often plagiarized the meaning of the Buddhadharma in order to discuss Confucianism, and then slandered the Buddhadharma besides. This is truly an offense. Yet what they plagiarized was only a half-understanding. Not only was it not the definitive meaning, it was not even the complete meaning. To slander on such a basis: how could that be right! The path by which they plagiarized was nothing other than the recorded sayings of the Chan school. In Chan practice, though the school takes prajñā as its foundation, because it does not rely on words, it does not develop its teaching on the basis of the scriptures. Moreover, what it says is uniformly lofty and undifferentiated, and it is here that it is easily plagiarized and forced into analogies. Yet that the fundamental and ultimate definitive meaning does not suffer being pulled about and thrown into confusion is also a fortunate consequence of this. Why? Confucians who restrain themselves and cultivate the person, who follow the rules and tread the proper path: are they not gentlemen? Yet their vision is short and shallow and their mental scope narrow; most of them, having gained a little, are smugly pleased, and knowing one point they deny the second. Hence since the Han dynasty, when the honor of Confucius was proclaimed, apart from the Han scholars' philological studies, which still benefited the Confucian books, others dragged in the sayings of apocryphal prophecy, or pulled in the doctrines of Huang-Lao, or plagiarized the leftover threads of the Chan school that resemble Confucian texts, forcing analogies and dressing them up in splendor. In truth they had not even dreamed of the genuine meaning of Confucianism. Yet the factional strife was noisily at its height. With men of such deep self-view, even if they heard the fundamental and ultimate definitive meaning of the Buddhadharma, their inability to grasp it may also be settled. Consider how the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi each drew near to great Chan masters for many years, and what they gained was no more than this. That they turned instead to raising spears against one another is enough to prove that my words are not mistaken! That being so, if such men had heard the teaching of the ultimate definitive meaning, even if they had not come to blows, they would surely have treated it as they treated Confucian principles, pulling in branches and leaves, plausible but false, so that the true meaning was obscured instead. This is again the greatest fortune within misfortune.

Further, these four sections contain another essential meaning that also must not go unclarified. What is that meaning? It is that the first section is the master, and the remaining three sections explain the reason why. How is the first section the master? "Prajñā-pāramitā is precisely not prajñā-pāramitā" is the master. One should know that prajñā is the wisdom everyone inherently possesses; it is precisely the pure mind. This pure mind has no place where it abides and leaves no trace when it is used; fundamentally it cannot be held and cannot be grasped. This is what is meant by the mind-moon standing alone in its roundness, its light swallowing all phenomena. Why? Because it is absolutely pure. Does the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment not say: "Where there is illumination and where there is awareness, both are called obstructions." The Buddha speaks prajñā in order to enable people to rely on the words, give rise to contemplation, and realize true reality. But he feared that people would retain the wisdom of illumination and awareness, and those of lower capacity might even seek prajñā within names and words. Therefore, precisely when explaining the reason for upholding it, he does not shrink from saying it himself and overturning it himself, declaring: "Prajñā is precisely not prajñā." Spoken thus, it straightaway leaves not a single word's footprint in the mind of the one who upholds it, and not a trace of any mark can adhere. This is truly what is meant by a sharp blade cutting through tangled hemp. This itself is the Diamond Prajñā, utterly different from the prajñā of resemblance. (Where the principle of prajñā is not seen through, the treatises call it prajñā of resemblance, meaning that it seems so but is not.) All practitioners should uphold it in this way.

Above it is said, "by this name": one should use this Diamond name. Therefore this Diamond Prajñā, upheld to break delusion, leaves no delusion unexhausted; upheld to illumine principle, leaves no principle unrevealed. Thus it can be identical with all dharmas and apart from all marks; and further, apart from all marks, it practices all dharmas. If one can truly uphold it in this way, then with regard to worldly and world-transcending dharmas alike one ultimately reaches their root and branch, their end and boundary. It is for this that it is called pāramitā. This is the true meaning of the Buddha's saying that prajñā is precisely not prajñā. Fearing again that students might not comprehend, he further speaks the next three sections to make its meaning clear, so that they may understand it thoroughly.

The section asking whether there is any dharma spoken makes clear that prajñā is without words and without speech. The statement above that prajñā is not prajñā precisely reveals that it cannot be reached by words and speech. Therefore the question whether there is any dharma spoken tests one's insight. The answer that nothing is spoken stands precisely opposed, point to point, to the intent of the question. If one understands that although he speaks all day and speaks ardently, in truth there are no words and no speech, then one does not seek it within words and speech. One who upholds it thus is practicing prajñā-pāramitā.

The section on the three-thousand great chiliocosm makes clear that in prajñā, object and wisdom are one suchness. That prajñā is not prajñā precisely reveals that prajñā is not really one dharma, and that every dharma is prajñā, making clear that all dharmas are one suchness. Fearing that this might not be understood, he borrows atoms and worlds to raise a question. The answer "very many" speaks of marks in terms of marks. And the Tathagata's saying "not" and saying "provisional name" means that precisely marks are without marks. If one awakens to the fact that the subtle atoms and the vast worlds are condition-arisen, without own-nature, and in their very substance are not, and are all provisional names, then every atom and every land is nothing but prajñā. This is what is meant by turning the great Dharma wheel within a single atom and establishing a jewel-king land on the tip of a hair. This is what is meant by the whole ten directions being one's own light, and by mountains and rivers with the great earth fully revealing the Dharma-king's body. All these express the meaning that object and wisdom are one suchness. When object and wisdom are one suchness, then there is no subject and no object, and one is absolutely pure. One who upholds it thus is practicing prajñā-pāramitā.

The section on the thirty-two marks makes clear that prajñā is without wisdom and without attainment. That prajñā is not prajñā precisely reveals prajñā as right wisdom: the enlightened nature, perfect and bright, with nothing that enlightens and nothing enlightened. But ordinary beings say: if there is no wisdom that realizes and no fruit realized, why do the thirty-two marks appear? Therefore he asks whether one can see the Tathagata by them. The answer "no" directly shows that the dharma-body is unconditioned and fundamentally not a physical mark. Yet because the Tathagata is without wisdom and without attainment, he accordingly follows conditions in great compassion and manifests boundless marks and excellences, whether thirty-two marks or even whatever form throughout the six paths. From this one knows that all the various marks and excellences are merely what follows conditions and appears. Since it is a gate of conditioned arising, marks are precisely not marks but are provisional names. Hence he says "not" and says "is called." If one understands that non-marks are provisional names, then the Tathagata may be seen everywhere. To see the Tathagata in the thirty-two marks is possible. But if not, and one clings to the thirty-two marks, one will in the end never see the Tathagata. Upholding prajñā is exactly so. In sum, the Dharma-gate of prajñā was originally spoken by the Tathagata. Now he shows that there is not even anything spoken: how much less the dharmas of prajñā. That one should not cling to them needs no saying. Dismissing the clinging to dharmas is because in the pure mind there must be no mark of an object. Hence he further shows that atoms are not atoms and worlds are not worlds, so that one knows that every dharma and every instance is nothing but prajñā, and there is no separate object. Yet the reason people do not forget the object of prajñā is that the Buddha realized this himself. Hence he further shows that one does not see the Tathagata by marks. If one knows that the thirty-two marks are non-marks and are provisional names, then one can see all marks as non-marks. If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata. Knowing this, the purport that prajñā is precisely not prajñā can be clearly illumined. And how it is to be upheld can also be clearly illumined. For in sum it is all shown so that one may uphold it by being precisely marks and apart from marks.

If the sections were divided according to this meaning and purport, then the second, third, and fourth sections should be placed under the first. The reason it is not done so here, but rather they are set out in parallel, is that by dividing them in parallel the meanings of not clinging to either emptiness or existence, and of dismissal and perfect fusion, are revealed clearly and are easier to comprehend. Yet the meaning that the section "prajñā is precisely not prajñā" is the master is plainly present in the sutra and must not be omitted; hence I add this explanation.

Besides this there is another meaning, also very essential, that must not go unknown. This section, the request for the name and the upholding, has already gone from subduing delusion to cutting off delusion. Yet one should know that delusion has coarse and subtle forms, and here what is cut off is the coarse delusion of discrimination. Hence the general judgment of the first half is: "By way of the object, making clear non-dwelling." What the latter half cuts off is the subtle delusion that is innate. Hence its general judgment is: "By way of the mind, making clear non-dwelling." Question: here it has already made clear freedom from thought: is this not already "by way of the mind"? Answer: there are two meanings here, differing between the earlier and later parts. (1) Although here it is already by way of the mind, it still belongs to the exposition of principle (that is, it still belongs to opening understanding). What follows belongs to the exposition of practice. In practice it further reveals meaning, to supply what is not yet reached here. This is one point of difference between earlier and later. (2) Here it first leaves coarse thought, that is, the thought of deliberate discrimination. What follows leaves subtle thought, that is, the thought that does not await discrimination and is innate together with the mind. This is another point of difference between earlier and later. The above detailed explanation of the reasons is now complete.
(Gui) 3. Concluding by revealing the merit of upholding. It divides into two: (Zi) 1. Comparing with the giving of life; next, making clear the abundance of the merit of upholding.
(Zi) 1. Comparing with the giving of life.
["Subhūti, if a good man or good woman gives away body and life as many times as the sands of the Ganges..."]

The giving of treasures is still outer wealth; here, however, one gives away body and life, which the Buddhist scriptures call inner wealth, far weightier than outer wealth. What sentient beings love most is the body; what they prize most is life. The body refers to the four limbs and so forth; even when these are harmed without yet touching life itself, it is already hard to do, how much more to give up one's life for sentient beings. And it is not one body and life only, but as many as the sands of the Ganges. In a single lifetime a person has only one body and life. Now he says one gives away body and life as many times as the sands of the Ganges: from this one knows that life after life, age after age, he constantly gives away body and life. How hard it is, and how great the merit and virtue! Yet if the mark of giving is not forgotten, it still belongs to outflows. Take those in the world who kill themselves to perfect benevolence: one never hears that they accomplished Buddhahood.
(Zi) 2. Making clear the abundance of the merit of upholding.
["If, further, there is a person who, from this sutra, receives and upholds even a four-line verse and so forth, and speaks it for others, his merit is very great."]

That receiving and upholding a single four-line verse and so forth surpasses the giving of body and life as many times as the sands of the Ganges: what principle is this? Moreover, the two earlier comparisons both used the giving of treasures as the measure of superiority; here it is further measured against the giving of body and life: what is the explanation? One should know that the first revelation of superiority was because pure faith had just been born, and so the merit and virtue of giving the treasures of a single great chiliocosm was used for comparison to reveal its surpassing excellence. The second revelation of superiority was because the wisdom of understanding had grown: one not only knew the object to be empty, but also knew that within the mind there is fundamentally no dust-object. Hence the merit and virtue of giving the treasures of immeasurable, boundless great chiliocosms was used for comparison to reveal its surpassing excellence. By this point the understanding of the meaning is still deeper: the Diamond Wisdom has already been opened. Once this wisdom is opened, one knows how to cut off deluded thoughts and abandon the root and trunk of birth and death, and one's work and practice are more inward than before. Therefore the comparison is not made with outer wealth but with inner wealth. For one who upholds and speaks even a four-line verse, if he can open the Diamond Wisdom and uphold the Diamond Prajñā in his practice, can cut off thought. Cutting off thought, he abandons the root and trunk of birth and death and transcends the ordinary to enter the sage. Compared with one who can only give up body and life through many lives and many kalpas yet cannot give up the root and trunk of birth and death, the distance cannot be reckoned in miles. Therefore the merit and virtue of upholding and speaking even a four-line verse of this sutra is greater than the merit and virtue of giving body and life as many times as the sands of the Ganges. For by this the Diamond Wisdom can be opened, and one may hope to transcend the ordinary and enter the sage; whereas that other person, not knowing to uphold and speak this sutra, has no way to open the Diamond Wisdom and remains an ordinary being who cannot escape the suffering of birth, death, and rebirth.

blocks.text: Chapter Fourteen: Leaving Marks and Quiescent Extinction

inline.s: (Xin) 4. Accomplishing the understanding and wisdom. It divides into two: (Ren) 1. The one at the occasion praises and encourages; next, the Tathagata confirms and elaborates. (Ren) 1 again divides into three: (Gui) 1. Stating the understanding; next, expressing praise and request; third, encouraging faith and understanding.
(Gui) 1. Stating the understanding.
["At that time Subhūti, having heard this sutra spoken, deeply understood the meaning and purport, and with tears and weeping spoke to the Buddha:"]

From the opening of the sutra to this point, all the principle and practice for subduing and cutting off the two clingings to self and dharma in their discriminated form have been expounded layer by layer, from shallow to deep, most thoroughly and clearly. Hence this section follows with the statement of deep understanding. That the one at the occasion declares himself in this way is nothing but the wish that the whole assembly may attain the same; hence he both praises and encourages. Why? The Buddha and the elder did not spare their painstaking words, repeatedly clarifying the purport of non-dwelling, originally because they wished those who heard to open a perfect understanding. For the sutra's purport is the supremely profound and wondrous supreme meaning of the middle way; if one does not comprehend its profundity and subtlety, one's insight is not perfect, and how can one be free of the two extremes and accord with the middle way? The sutra says, "deeply understood the meaning and purport," which precisely makes clear that his insight was already perfect and no longer the one-sided emptiness of before. This is why he declares of himself that it was not by the wisdom-eye alone that he heard it, and comes to tears and weeping. Although this speaks of understanding the meaning, in fact it already includes practice. For understanding and practice can never be separated; hence it is said that understanding and practice advance together. They advance together because one must practice to the point before one can understand to the point, and one must understand perfectly before practice is perfect.

One should know that cultivation is nothing other than the three wisdoms of hearing, reflecting, and cultivating. Thus hearing this sutra spoken here is the wisdom of hearing. (Why this hearing is the wisdom of hearing will be explained below.) And deep understanding is the wisdom of reflecting and the wisdom of cultivating. Why? Because without reflecting and cultivating contemplation one cannot deeply understand. Hence it is said that speaking of understanding includes practice. Nor is this all. What is the meaning and purport of this "deeply understood the meaning and purport"? It is to have deeply grasped why the text above says how one should generate faith and how one should uphold it. That being so, to speak of the one word "understanding" includes not only practice but also faith. And the text below says: "When the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born." The birth of true reality is the realization of the nature. The text below also says: "To hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it is foremost and rare." And further: "Why? Being apart from all marks, they are called Buddhas." Calling them Buddhas makes clear that they have realized the nature. That being so, to speak of one "deep understanding" includes not only faith and cultivation but realization as well. Moreover, the meaning that when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born, further says that the birth of true reality is precisely the purity of the mind of faith. Seeing this, the faith, understanding, practice, and realization spoken of before, though spoken of as four matters, are in fact one that is four and four that are one, and this principle is all the more proved.

This passage on accomplishing the understanding and wisdom is the place where everything from the opening of the sutra converges. Why? All the repeated questions and answers between teacher and disciple above, the painstaking words and heartfelt care used to bring out the supremely profound meaning and purport: what was their purpose? Nothing but the hope that those who hear the Dharma may open a deep understanding. Is it not the case that all the thousands of words above find their resting place only in this section? Hence it is called the place of convergence. Nor is this all. From the next section, "the Tathagata confirms and elaborates," onward, everything the World-Honored One says is nothing but developing and proving the essential points already stated above, causing people to gain a further layer of faith and understanding regarding the essential purport already spoken, so that their upholding becomes more effective. Therefore this fourth section, accomplishing the understanding and wisdom, together with the fifth section below, supremely revealing the sutra's merit, are the summarizing text of the first half. These are the veins and eyes of the sutra, so I bring them out in advance and point them out beforehand, so that when one comes to the text it is easier to understand.

It is the custom of this sutra that wherever the compiler of the sutra marks a passage with "at that time" and so forth, it indicates a new beginning. Here the four characters "deeply understood the meaning and purport," as to the meaning and purport, are all present in the text above; but as to deep understanding, this is absent from the text above and is only now declared by the elder himself, hence it is called a new beginning. The two characters "at that time" correspond exactly to the "at that time" in the earlier request for the name and the upholding. For before the request for the name and the upholding, the meaning made clear was the opening of the wisdom that knows the object to be empty and the wisdom that is free of dust. At the request for the name and the upholding, the Diamond Wisdom was opened. This wisdom is most profound and not easily grasped. If this wisdom is opened, one cuts off delusion and realizes the true, and this is where the work of cultivation returns. Now to say "deeply understood the meaning and purport" is to declare of oneself that one has opened the Diamond Wisdom. If one had opened only the wisdom that knows the object to be empty and the wisdom that is free of dust, that would be no more than the stage of contemplation and practice or the stage of resemblance, and could not be called deep understanding. Nor is this all. The "at that time" here corresponds directly to the "at that time" at the beginning of the sutra, when the elder Subhūti rose from his seat in the midst of the assembly. Why? Without that earlier request for the Dharma, how could there be this deep understanding now? If one looks deeply, this deep understanding was already latent in that earlier request for the Dharma. Why? Because the elder alone, when the great assembly was blind and dull, could see through to the fact that the Buddha did not dwell in marks, and therefore requested the Dharma. Hence on hearing the Dharma he understood at once. Anyone else could never hear this sutra spoken and immediately attain deep understanding of its meaning and purport. This is why the text below says it is not difficult. Thus the sutra's text already plainly points out the connection between earlier and later. Nor is this all. At that moment he opened his mouth and at once praised what was rare; at this moment too he opens his mouth and at once praises what is rare. Both point out the eye of the connection between earlier and later. Further, consider how at that time the elder rose from his seat, wishing and delighting to hear, how joyous and eager he was; while at this time the elder is in tears and weeping. The earlier and later set each other off, and there is great significance in this. For the joy of that time is precisely the root of the weeping of this time. As for the two characters "at that time," if spoken of as the present moment, it is the time when the explanation of why one should uphold it has just concluded, and also the time when, having heard and deeply understood, grief wells up from within. The "heard" of "heard this sutra spoken" corresponds exactly to "wishing and delighting to hear" at the beginning of the sutra. To hear what one wished to hear, and further to understand it deeply: this is truly a blessing of ten thousand, and this is why joy to the utmost becomes sorrow. Deep understanding corresponds to the attentive listening at the very beginning; without attentive listening, deep understanding is utterly impossible. Hence the "heard" of "heard this sutra spoken" is not hearing in a loose sense; it is what is called the wisdom of hearing. Yet this too is said of the elder, because he was originally the foremost arhat free from desire, long able to be without thought, and possessed both the wisdom-eye and the foremost understanding of emptiness. Therefore before he had heard this sutra he could already penetrate the purport of non-dwelling and see the Tathagata. Hence the effect of attentive listening was most great, and on hearing he understood deeply. As for an ordinary being, even if he can listen attentively, he can never awaken thoroughly at a single stroke. To open the wisdom that knows the object to be empty is already rare and admirable. To hear the sutra and straightaway be free of dust: how many in a thousand ages could do so. As for the Diamond Wisdom, there is no need to speak of it. Even the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Master of the Chan school, awakened suddenly on hearing "give rise to the mind that dwells nowhere." In ancient and modern times there has been no second such person. Yet after transmitting the robe and bowl he was still entangled among hunters for more than ten years. This was precisely the Buddhas and patriarchs adding their blessing and tempering the diamond sword of his wisdom. In the final age it is difficult beyond difficulty. Hence the text below says: in the last five hundred years, to hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such a person is rare. This principle must not go unknown. Yet one must also not block oneself because of the difficulty. The Buddha says that in the last five hundred years those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit can give rise to faith, and can then respond in a single thought. Faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit and virtue; if one can truly believe on hearing the sutra, one enters the gate of prajñā. Having entered the gate, why could one not awaken suddenly and cut off suddenly? Why? Because the Buddhas add their blessing, and because one's past wisdom is profound. What then is meant by entering the gate? Truly believing that the dust-objects are all empty and not being bound by them: this is the initial gate of prajñā. This principle especially must not go unknown.

"Meaning" is principle. That is, the true meaning of the gates of contemplation and the gates of practice spoken of above, whether subduing or cutting off. "Purport" is the place of return, also called the direction. That is, what the text below calls "when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born." For the principles are manifold, but their place of return is one. The Buddha speaks the prajñā of words for no other reason than to enable one to rely on it, give rise to contemplation, and realize true reality. If one does not understand where the meaning returns, one is like counting sand in the sea, with nothing to conclude. One is also like a boat without a rudder: where will it go? Then there is no benefit or effect to speak of. Therefore to understand the meaning but not the purport is not deep understanding. Moreover, as to the purport, if one understands only where it returns but not how to move toward it, one is still like counting another's treasure, with not half a coin as one's own portion, and this too is not deep understanding. One must both understand where the meaning returns and further understand how to move toward that place: only this is truly deep understanding. These four characters, "deeply understood the meaning and purport," were added by the compiler of the sutra. For from the elder's declaration below, one can know that he was able to grasp and understand deeply; hence they are specially marked out. This marking out has two purposes: (1) to let readers of the sutra know that what is said in the declaration below is the place of return of all the wondrous meanings since the opening of the sutra, and should be pondered with wholehearted attention; (2) if it were not marked out, from where would the tears and weeping come? And it lets one know that the elder, foremost in understanding emptiness, wept because he deeply understood this sutra, showing that the emptiness spoken of in the sutra is not the ordinary emptiness that stands opposed to existence. It also lets one know that the elder, a great disciple who personally attended beneath the Buddha's seat, came to weep on hearing and understanding this sutra. This shows that this sutra is truly hard to encounter and hard to meet; how could it be taken lightly, and how much less could it be read without wholehearted attention. It also lets one know that the elder's weeping came from deep understanding. This shows that those who read this sutra long and remain unmoved at heart, who even fear to speak of prajñā, have no other reason than this: they have not grasped the meaning and purport within the sutra. Speaking thus, the compiler of the sutra specially marked out this sentence, and its admonition is most profound and most urgent.

"With tears and weeping" precisely makes clear his sorrow. Tears are the outward form of weeping. Weeping and wailing differ: tears with sound is wailing, tears without sound is weeping. The reason people wail is that they suddenly suffer a great loss from beyond expectation, as though a knife cut the heart, and in utter dismay they cannot keep from crying out in anguish; this is called wailing. The reason people weep is that they deeply rejoice at gaining what they had not gained, joy and shame intermingled, gratitude to the utmost, and they cannot keep from shedding tears in sorrow; this is called weeping. The elder's arising of sorrow is no different from this. Because he looks at the present and rejoices, and looks back at the past and feels shame, and being both shamed and joyful he therefore feels all the more the Buddha's grace. These three states of mind together bring forth the outward form of weeping. How can this be seen? Here it says "having heard," and joining this with the text below, where the Buddha says "such a profound scripture" and "in former days I never heard it," then his gratitude today that the Buddha spoke it for him, and his deep joy at the blessing of hearing it, can be known. And though in former days he had the wisdom-eye, he had not heard this sutra, and his deep sense of shame is plainly laid bare. One should know that where he laments the past is precisely where he rejoices in the present. Hence it is said: the elder's arising of sorrow is what these three states of mind, joy, shame, and gratitude, bring forth. As for what is said in the three exhortations to faith and understanding below, there the elder not only rejoices for himself but rejoices further that all sentient beings will obtain the supreme treasure; this is why he widely encourages faith, understanding, receiving, and upholding. That being so, with joy and shame thus intermingled, how could he not be moved to tears?

When ordinary people first awaken from the great dream and recall the past, is it not all like the silkworm making its cocoon and binding itself, like the moth rushing into the flame and burning itself? Looking at the present and thinking of the past, they often cannot keep from weeping. An ancient worthy said: "While the great matter is not yet clear, one is as though bereaved of father and mother; when the great matter is clear, one is all the more as though bereaved of father and mother." Both say the same thing. As for "spoke to the Buddha," it is because, on hearing this sutra spoken, he attained deep understanding of the meaning and purport; because of this deep understanding he came to tears and weeping; and thereupon he declared his insight and sought the Buddha's confirmation. This is a matter of course. Reading the eight characters "with tears and weeping spoke to the Buddha" together, it means he spoke while shedding tears. Looking at how at the beginning of the sutra the elder requested the Dharma for the great assembly, and how below he widely encourages faith and understanding, one can see that when the elder spoke to the World-Honored One with tears, he was speaking with tears to all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm and to the end of the future. What the next section says, that in former days his wisdom-eye had never heard it, is likewise addressed to all sentient beings everywhere. Our elder's great compassion and great mercy intend to admonish all sentient beings to quickly bring forth the unsurpassed bodhi mind and uphold prajñā: only thus do they continue and prosper the Buddha-seed, and only thus do they not betray their own spirit. If one studies the small Dharma, then even one who, like me, has opened the wisdom-eye, attained the samādhi of non-contention, and become the foremost arhat free from desire, still cannot escape this sense of past and present. Be careful not to be like me, regretting that one heard the Way too late. And the Buddha's speaking of this sutra is hard to meet in ten thousand kalpas. Moreover, its meaning and purport are most profound; if one is able to hear it, one should uphold it according to the Dharma and seek deep understanding. Only then does one know that the Buddha's grace is hard to repay, and one rejoices and is at ease for a lifetime. In sum, the elder's joy is joy for sentient beings; the elder's gratitude is gratitude for sentient beings; his shame over the past and his weeping declaration are all meant to inspire sentient beings. One should know that in our attaining the hearing of this most profound scripture, not only is the Buddha's grace hard to repay, the elder's grace is also hard to repay. Why? Because the Buddha spoke this sutra only because the elder requested it on behalf of sentient beings.
(Gui) 2. Expressing praise and rejoicing.
["Rare, World-Honored One! The Buddha speaks such a profound scripture. From of old, the wisdom-eye I had attained had never heard such a sutra."]

"Rare" appears twice, and though the words of praise are the same, the meaning of the praise differs. The first was because he had just awakened to the original face, like a person suddenly beholding a treasure hard to obtain; hence he praised it as rare. Now he has deeply understood the true meaning and purport, like a person who has already gained wealth beyond expectation (in former days he had not heard it, and now he hears it, hence beyond expectation), rejoicing exceedingly; hence he praises it as rare. For the first was seeing the great plan from outside, and this is peering into the inner chamber.

These two characters "rare" not only praise the Buddha but also praise the Dharma, and further contain the meaning of rejoicing for oneself. The text below says "the Buddha speaks such a sutra," from which one can know that it praises the rarity of the Buddha's speaking. This also contains four meanings. (1) What is hard to speak, he can speak. The supremely profound prajñā only the Buddhas with the Buddhas ultimately realize, and so only the Buddhas with the Buddhas can ultimately speak it. And a single Buddha's appearance in the world must pass through many kalpas; hence it is called rare. (2) It is spoken only when the time has come. This Diamond Sutra was spoken at the ninth assembly of the Prajñā, and without the elder as the one at the occasion, to whom would it have been spoken? For speech must meet the right vessel; if the karmic conditions are not ripe, speaking brings no benefit. Hence it is called rare. (3) Without speaking, he speaks. The Tathagata has nothing spoken; the Buddha's speaking of this is originally to enable sentient beings to see the Tathagata. Moreover, prajñā fundamentally cannot be reached by words and speech; hence although now he speaks ardently, one should know it is truly the speaking of no speaking, speaking yet not speaking. Hence it is called rare. (4) He speaks because of great compassion. The Buddha sees sentient beings as fundamentally Buddhas; because they have obscured their original nature, they have become sentient beings, and so he calls them pitiable. Hence though this unconditioned Dharma cannot be spoken, he provisionally establishes all kinds of skillful means and speaks it, all to cause them to enter nirvāṇa without residue and be delivered. Is this not rare?

As for praising the Dharma as well, the text below says "the Buddha speaks such a profound scripture," and the two characters "profound" are words of praise. To call the scripture profound makes clear that it surpasses other scriptures. The unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Dharma is hard to encounter in a hundred thousand million kalpas. As the text above of this sutra says: "All Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra," and that upholding and speaking even a four-line verse and so forth surpasses the giving of body and life as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and even that wherever this sutra is, there is the Buddha, or a revered disciple, and so forth: from these the rarity of this Dharma can be known. As for what is said later, that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and that it is spoken for those who have brought forth the supreme vehicle, and so forth: all make clear that it is a rare Dharma. Since they all come later in the text, I do not cite and explain them here.

How does it contain the meaning of rejoicing for oneself? As the text below says, the wisdom-eye of former days had not heard these words: this is precisely rejoicing for himself that he now hears and deeply understands. That being so, why was the eye of the Way not opened formerly, and why is his insight deep now? Is this not a rare matter?

Why is it called a profound scripture? What this sutra speaks is the fundamental meaning of the Buddhadharma, the ultimate definitive meaning, the supreme meaning of the middle way of great wisdom, great compassion, great vows, and great practice; it is the meaning of the emptiness of the supreme meaning; it is the meaning that enables those who believe, understand, receive, and uphold it to become Buddhas. Moreover, every word and every character contains inexhaustible meaning, and its depth has no bottom; hence it is called profound. That the wisdom-eye of the foremost arhat free from desire had never heard it precisely makes clear how profound it is. Further, prajñā-pāramitā is deep, and this sutra is the Diamond Prajñā-pāramitā; hence it is profound. As for the other sayings cited above, that the Buddha and the Buddhadharma all come forth from this sutra, and so forth, their profundity can be known.

"From of old" means from the time he realized the fruit of arhatship and attained the wisdom-eye. What is the wisdom-eye? "Eye" means insight. The Buddhist scriptures speak of five eyes. (1) The flesh-eye, which is the insight of ordinary beings. (2) The heaven-eye, which is the insight of gods and humans. Gods and humans are also ordinary beings, but what they see surpasses that of the human path and below; hence it is called the heaven-eye. (3) The wisdom-eye: seeing the principle of the emptiness of the person is called the wisdom-eye. This is the insight of the arhat. (4) The dharma-eye: having seen the emptiness of the person, one further sees the emptiness of dharmas; hence it is called the dharma-eye. This is the insight of the bodhisattva. (5) The Buddha-eye: this means the Buddha's knowledge and vision, and it surpasses all. Here I briefly state their outline; when the text below explains the five eyes, I will give details.

From of old he had emptied only the person and the self, whereas this sutra empties the dharma-self. Hence he had never entered this principle. Therefore he says that from of old the wisdom-eye had never heard it. This contains many and most essential meanings. I should now analyze and explain them.

(1) Above it says "eye," and below it says "heard": eye and hearing have no connection at all. This proves that the so-called eye means insight, and cannot be taken as the eye of eye and ear, nor as the seeing of eye-seeing.

(2) Since eye and hearing have no connection, the so-called hearing likewise cannot be taken rigidly as hearing with the ear. It is the hearing of turning the hearing back to hear the self-nature, what is called the wisdom of hearing.

(3) Since it is the wisdom of hearing, then to speak of hearing is to speak of understanding. That being so, "formerly never heard" does not mean that he never heard at all; it means that although he heard, he did not attain understanding, which is equal to never having heard.

(4) His shame that in the past he had not heard it is precisely his joy that now he has heard it. How does he hear it now? Through his deep understanding. Hence above he says, "the Buddha speaks such a profound scripture." Why? Because without deep understanding, one would not know that this sutra is thus profound. This is why the compiler of the sutra marked it with the words "deeply understood the meaning and purport."

(5) The elder's sigh that in the past he had not heard it carries much of the sentiment of regretting that he heard the Way too late; this is why he wept just now. That being so, how is it that now he hears and deeply understands? Because he observed that the Tathagata, being non-dwelling with regard to dharmas, did not grasp the dharmas he had formerly studied, as can be known. And further, because he requested this great Dharma for the assembly, his bringing forth of the mind of great wisdom, great practice, great compassion, and great vows can be known. His insight was utterly different from before; hence he could penetrate this profoundly deep sutra.

(6) This sutra was spoken at the ninth assembly of the Great Prajñā Sutra; why then say that in the past he had never heard it? Moreover, in the first eight assemblies the elder even taught the bodhisattvas in turn, so one cannot say that in the past he had not opened understanding. One should know that the elder speaks thus for no other reason than to exhort sentient beings to rise quickly and read and recite this sutra, to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it.

(7) As for the eight assemblies of the past, he had indeed heard them. In teaching the bodhisattvas in turn, he had indeed opened understanding. But the Diamond Prajñā is spoken only at this point. Hence it is called profound, and hence it is said that in the past he had never heard it.

(8) Speaking thus, the deep understanding spoken of above is a most profound understanding. For prajñā is already a profound scripture, and in the earlier assemblies he had already taught the bodhisattvas, so he had long since opened deep understanding. Yet the sutra of this assembly is a most profound scripture; hence the understanding of today is a most profound understanding. Therefore he cannot keep from looking at the present and thinking of the past, and knowing that only such comprehension is thorough. This is why he regretted hearing the Way too late, this is why he came to tears and weeping, and this is why he widely encouraged faith and understanding.

(9) There is a further subtle intent in the elder's declaring himself thus. What is that intent? To show the great assembly that with so profound a scripture one must never cling to the words, and never seek outwardly. One should gather the ear into the mind, reflect back upon the self-nature, and only then open one's insight and understand the profound meaning and purport within the sutra.

(10) Nor is this all. There is a deeper intent here. Since it is the eye of the emptiness of the person, it cannot see the principle of the emptiness of dharmas. From this one can see that in a person's study of the Way, the stages of shallow and deep admit not the slightest forcing. And the elder's eye of the Way had to wait until the ninth assembly before it opened. From this one can further see that time and karmic conditions likewise admit not the slightest forcing. Nor is this all. The World-Honored One appeared in the world originally to enable sentient beings to realize the wisdom of prajñā and reach the shore of nirvāṇa. Yet he delayed long before speaking prajñā, and delayed long again before speaking the Diamond Prajñā. From this one can see that even one who brings forth the great compassion mind cannot be impatient, because the vessel and the teaching must fit together. And one who had the insight of a wisdom-eye still could not hear it. From this one can further see that in reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, one must sweep away all one's past preconceptions before there is hope of penetrating. For as soon as there is a preconception, it obstructs the eye of the Way.

(Gui) 3. Encouraging faith and understanding. It divides into two: (Zi) 1. Encouraging by way of the present; next, encouraging by way of the future. (Zi) 1 again divides into two: (Chou) 1. Making clear the accomplishment; next, making clear true reality.
(Chou) 1. Making clear the accomplishment.

["World-Honored One, if again there is a person who hears this sutra, and whose mind of faith is pure, then true reality is born in him. One should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rare merit and virtue."]

The elder's great compassion, having itself obtained the joy of the Dharma, universally wishes that all sentient beings of the present and the future may obtain the joy of the Dharma together. Hence he fully sets out the rarity of the accomplishment, so that the great assembly, hearing it, may bring forth the mind of faith and understanding. Though the text does not plainly say "I exhort," the intent to exhort is earnest. This is precisely the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened bodhi mind of great compassion and great vows. "If again there is a person": this is a deep hope that there may be such a person. "Hears this sutra" contains the sense that it is not easily obtained, that one is fortunate to obtain it, and that one must not let this one obtaining slip by. Purity is precisely being without marks. As before, taking non-dwelling in the six dusts as the generation of the pure mind precisely makes clear that dwelling in dust is clinging to marks. The slightest clinging to marks is no longer purity. And since it says both "non-dwelling" and "generating the mind," it further makes clear that what is called "without marks" is not the absence spoken of in contrast to presence, but an absolute absence. That is, when the four propositions of existence, non-existence, both, and neither are all absent, only then is it the true exposition of no marks. To speak thoroughly, when even this absolute absence is also absent, only then is it ultimate purity. Therefore one who reaches the first abode realizes only a single portion of the pure mind; from there, as work and practice advance, the more they advance the subtler they become, passing through forty stages, until the stage of equal enlightenment, where there still remains one portion of the most subtle ignorance. In other words, the pure mind still falls slightly short; hence it is said that at equal enlightenment one sees the nature as though looking at the moon through a gauze. One must further remove this with the Diamond Wisdom before one becomes the ultimate enlightenment, and then the pure mind is fully manifested.

Why is it called "the mind of faith is pure"? It means that by believing in this prajñā of words, one gives rise to the prajñā of contemplation and thereby attains a single, unified purity of mind. Hence this one phrase, "the mind of faith is pure," though it speaks only of the one word "faith," includes understanding, practice, and realization as well. Without contemplative wisdom, how could clinging be dismissed? Without dismissing again and again until one reaches absolute absence, how could the mind of faith become pure? What is called contemplative wisdom is precisely upholding the Diamond Prajñā, being apart from names and words, not clinging to any subtle or vast object, and not clinging even to the hope for a surpassing fruit. One simply goes straight on practicing according to the Dharma, with not a single thought arising. If one can truly cut off one portion of deluded marks and thoughts (that is, the mind of arising and ceasing, which is also thought), then the pure mind manifests one portion. Manifesting one portion is realizing one portion of the dharma-body and ascending to the first abode, turning from ordinary to sage. From there one adds effort until the ultimate enlightenment, and afterwards arising and ceasing ceases and quiescent extinction appears. Then the self-nature's pure mind is perfectly manifested, which is called wondrous enlightenment, also called becoming a Buddha, also called entering nirvāṇa without residue. From this one can further see that the saying "faith is the gate of entry to the path" uses "gate" in a broad sense, not referring only to the great gate, but taking in the gate of the hall and the gate of the chamber without omission. One can further see that understanding, practice, and realization are three other names for the word "faith." In other words, understanding, practice, and realization are nothing else: they are simply faith gradually growing and brightening until it is ultimately firm and perfect. Why? To speak of understanding, practice, and realization, faith must be complete before understanding can be complete, practice complete, and realization complete. If faith falls at all short, how can one speak of being able to understand, to practice, to realize? Hence it is said that faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit and virtue. Therefore what was said above, that faith, understanding, practice, and realization should be viewed as perfectly fused, means they cannot be taken rigidly as four separate pegs. Hence in this sutra the three sections of opening understanding, advancing in practice, and accomplishing realization all speak of faith as well. This principle must not go unknown.

True reality is another name for the nature-body. The three lines below, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark; therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality," are themselves the explanation of this meaning. Why the nature-body is named true reality will be explained below; here I pass over it for the moment. The nature is inherently possessed, unborn and not non-born. To speak now of "born" means "appearing before one." This is the same as the earlier meaning of "generating the pure mind." Formerly, because it was in bondage, it did not appear. Now, upholding the Diamond Prajñā, the clouds of delusion gradually disperse and the light gradually shows, like the bright moon just risen. Since there is no way to name it, it is provisionally called "born." This is what the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom calls "the non-born born." "The non-born born" means being born without birth. The treatise also says: "All dharmas are unborn, yet prajñā is born." This means that if one understands that all dharmas are unborn, then the contemplative wisdom of non-arising appears before one; this is being born without birth.

This meaning is most profound, and I fear it may still not be understood. Let me explain it further: the contemplative wisdom of non-arising is precisely prajñā. Both prajñā and true reality are names of dharmas. Since all dharmas are unborn and prajñā is born, and prajñā is also one of all dharmas, how can it be said to be born? It merely makes clear that the contemplative wisdom of non-arising appears before one. For dharmas are fundamentally unborn, and are provisionally called born. Hence it is said, "this is being born without birth." Once the meaning of prajñā's being born is clear, the meaning of true reality's being born can be understood clearly. One should further know that prajñā and true reality are indeed names of dharmas, but this dharma is nothing other than the nature itself. Hence the phrase in this sutra, "true reality is born," is the manifestation of the nature's light. And the phrase in the great treatise, "prajñā is born," is the appearing of the contemplative wisdom of non-arising. The nature is fundamentally unborn; hence the phrase "contemplative wisdom of non-arising" is another way of saying "the wisdom of the nature." The wisdom of the nature is the nature's light. Why say "contemplative wisdom"? To make clear that this wisdom appears through contemplation. It is just like the words in this sutra, "the mind of faith is pure" making clear that the mind is pure because faith is accomplished. The sutra says "then is born"; "then" means "namely." The mind of faith being pure, true reality is born, is like saying that the mind of faith being pure is true reality appearing before one. Because faith is accomplished, the mind is pure. And the pure mind and true reality are both the original nature. Hence the mind of faith being pure is true reality appearing before one. This precisely reveals the meaning that its birth is no birth. One should know that to speak of purity is precisely because all dharmas are unborn. That being so, if there is the slightest birth, it is not the pure mind, as can be known. Yet it is further named "born" because it is born without birth, and its birth is no birth. Since the mind of faith being pure is true reality appearing before one, one can know that true reality appearing before one is likewise simply the mind of faith being pure. That being so, what is called realization can also be known to be a provisional name. In truth there is nothing realized and nothing attained. Nor is this all. What is called "the mind of faith is pure" is also what others say of him. In that person's mind he does not for a moment think himself accomplished in faith, nor for a moment think his mind pure. Why? If there is the slightest shadow remaining, it is a dharma-mark, it is clinging, and it is not the non-arising of all dharmas; how then could it be called accomplishment of faith and purity of mind?

That being so, why must the sutra text speak a word "born"? Why not simply say, "when the mind of faith is pure, true reality appears before one"? Would that not be more direct? One should know that to speak the word "born" further contains essential meanings.

(1) To speak of it as "born" makes clear that the purity of the mind of faith is a complete release from the senses and their objects, with the nature's light blazing forth, and is not like dead water.
