This carries the same sense as the earlier phrase "generating the pure mind." For it shows that what is called purity is quiescence and illumination at once, not quiescence alone without illumination. And to speak the one word "faith" further shows the work and practice, including the three matters of understanding, practice, and realization spoken of before.

(2) To speak of it as "born" makes clear the sense that it has just come to appear before one. For true reality must appear portion by portion and cannot suddenly be perfect. If one simply said "true reality appears before one," that would be too vague. Hence the word "born" is spoken, so that one may understand it as the moon just rising in the east.

(3) To speak of it as "born" further makes clear that one has just attained the turning from ordinary to sage. For true reality has only just appeared before one, which is to have manifested one portion. And to manifest one portion of true reality is to realize one portion of the dharma-body and to ascend to the first abode, which is the first step of the stage of partial realization. This is the stage of first becoming a bodhisattva. Hence the word "born" is spoken to show that one has just entered the sage's stage. Therefore the text below immediately continues: "One should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rare merit and virtue."

Did not the earlier explanation of "the most supreme, foremost, and rare" say: the most supreme is the unsurpassed, the foremost is the perfectly equal. The bodhisattva saves himself and saves others, self and others equal. And further, compassion and wisdom both in motion, merit and wisdom both cultivated, concentration and wisdom equally upheld: all these are the bodhisattva's work of cultivation, and all are the meaning of equality. "Perfectly equal" means that he is both rightly awakened and equal. In the Buddha's assembly the bodhisattva's stage is first, the small vehicle's stage is second. Hence "foremost" refers to the perfectly equal bodhisattva. "Rare" is right awakening. Ordinary beings are deluded and not awakened; outer-path practitioners' awakening is not right. Hence right awakening refers to the arhat of the small vehicle, making clear that he can awaken himself by the right Dharma. Because he can awaken himself by the right Dharma, he is called rare. "Rare" is spoken in contrast to ordinary beings and outer-path practitioners. If a bodhisattva not only awakens himself but can also awaken others, he is called perfectly equal. Spoken in full, this is perfect equal right awakening, which is also the foremost and rare. The Buddha awakens himself and awakens others, with the work of awakening complete; hence he is called unsurpassed, perfectly equal, right awakening, which is also the most supreme, foremost, and rare. Here the text says "accomplishes the foremost and rare merit and virtue" and does not say "most supreme," which makes clear that he has already become a bodhisattva, that is, a bodhisattva of the first abode. Because his true reality has only just been born, viewing the meaning of the text here all the more proves that the earlier "most supreme, foremost, and rare" should be explained as unsurpassed, perfectly equal awakening, and cannot be explained otherwise. Further, the "foremost" here can indeed also be explained as becoming the first-stage bodhisattva of the first abode; but this is not appropriate, because it would not be consistent with the earlier "most supreme, foremost, and rare," and it is better to keep the explanation as perfectly equal.

As for speaking of merit and virtue: "merit" is the work of cultivation, "virtue" is the virtue of the nature. This makes clear that since one has already become a sage, illumination and awareness increase in brightness. Speaking in terms of breaking the delusions of self and other, the function is equal: this is the merit of accomplishing the foremost and rare. Speaking in terms of awakening oneself and awakening others, the nature's virtue first shows: this is the virtue of accomplishing the foremost and rare. Are merit-and-fortune and merit-and-virtue the same or different? Answer: one cannot definitively say they are the same, nor definitively say they are different. Why? Merit-and-fortune speaks specifically of fortune, while merit-and-virtue includes both fortune and wisdom; merit-and-fortune speaks of the karmic reward that is attracted, while merit-and-virtue speaks of the body and function that are revealed; merit-and-fortune is mostly spoken of as conditioned, while merit-and-virtue is mostly spoken of as unconditioned. This is why one cannot definitively say they are the same. Yet if one cultivates merit-and-virtue while clinging to marks, then merit-and-virtue becomes merit-and-fortune. If one cultivates merit-and-fortune without clinging to marks, then merit-and-fortune is precisely merit-and-virtue. This is why one cannot definitively say they are different.

Above, all the places comparing and revealing spoke of merit-and-fortune; here it speaks of merit-and-virtue. Why? Answer: wherever the text compares and reveals, it speaks of merit-and-fortune and not merit-and-virtue; there are three meanings in this. (1) Upholding and speaking this sutra is originally merit-and-virtue and not merit-and-fortune. But because the comparison is drawn from the merit-and-fortune of mark-clinging giving, following the convenience of the text, it is for the moment also named merit-and-fortune. (2) It also serves to make clear that one who practices non-dwelling, though he should not cling to marks, should also not destroy marks. Hence in every case it speaks of merit-and-fortune, to show the meaning that one who cultivates wisdom should also cultivate fortune. (3) The reason upholding and speaking this sutra surpasses mark-clinging giving is nothing else: it is precisely because one comprehends the principle of not clinging to marks. Hence it speaks in every case of merit-and-fortune, to make clear that if one does not cling to marks, merit-and-fortune is precisely merit-and-virtue. One should further know that those who give the seven treasures or give body and life were originally people who had brought forth the great mind, that is, people cultivating merit-and-virtue; otherwise they could never have given in this way. Yet it is said only to be merit-and-fortune for no other reason than that, not upholding and speaking this sutra, they cannot comprehend the principle that one should not cling to marks. Thus it further contains the meaning that if they cling to marks, merit-and-virtue becomes merit-and-fortune. As for this place, it is not drawing a comparison from mark-clinging merit-and-fortune, but rather revealing that when the mind of faith is pure, one accomplishes the foremost and rare. One should know that because he can be free of clinging to marks, he can be pure and attain such accomplishment. Hence one cannot speak of merit-and-fortune here, but only of merit-and-virtue.

The section above was the elder declaring of himself that he was already able to understand deeply. If not deep understanding, how would he know the scripture to be profound? This meaning has been discussed in detail before. Yet to make clear only the deep understanding is still a general statement. From this section down to "are called Buddhas," he then sets out clearly the meaning and purport he has deeply understood. If one speaks only of this section, then the phrase "the mind of faith is pure" is the deep understanding of the meaning and also contains the sense of deeply understanding the purport. "Then true reality is born; one should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rare merit and virtue" precisely makes clear the deep understanding of the purport. "One should know" means one should know that the birth of true reality is precisely the accomplishment. And further, one should know that when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born. The two characters "one should know," though placed in the middle, carry the meaning through both ends. To say "one should know" is precisely because he himself has attained deep understanding, and so he exhorts others likewise to understand deeply.

Why is "the mind of faith is pure" the deep understanding of the meaning? Because in the earlier passage on generating faith, the World-Honored One said that keeping the precepts and cultivating merit can give rise to faith, and one takes this as true. Then he continues: "hearing such words and chapter-and-verse, even a single thought gives rise to pure faith." And in the passage on opening understanding he further says, "one should generate a pure mind." Hence the elder now says "the mind of faith is pure," which corresponds exactly to the text above. The elder takes it that the World-Honored One from the first opening of his mouth has one bring forth the mind to save beings, saving boundless sentient beings while in truth no being attains deliverance, and that where there is the mark of self or person one is not a bodhisattva: this meaning is precisely to cause one not to grasp marks. What follows further has one give without dwelling in the six dusts and generate the mind without dwelling in the six dusts, which is nothing but causing one not to grasp marks. And why can one not grasp marks? Because one should generate the pure mind. What is called "a single thought gives rise to pure faith": how is faith pure? The mind is pure. From this one sees that to give rise to pure faith is to give rise to the pure mind. One further sees that the purity of the mind comes entirely from faith. Consider the phrase "a single thought gives rise to pure faith": its intent is to make clear that one has already attained a single thought of response. What is response? It is that in a single thought one responds to the self-nature's pure mind. The meaning of response is realization. And without practice, how could there be realization; without understanding, how could there be practice. Yet understanding, practice, and realization are not mentioned at all; it says only that a single thought gives rise to pure faith. From this one sees that the single word "faith" already penetrates to the very bottom. It is to make people understand that if one can truly believe as the cause, one must obtain the fruit of pure faith. In brief: as faith grows to perfection, the mind becomes pure. Viewed thus, the elder's one phrase, "the mind of faith is pure," is no different from the crystallization of all the meanings the World-Honored One spoke above. Without deeply understanding their meaning, he could not have uttered it.

The text above further says: "When a single thought gives rise to pure faith, the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees it; such sentient beings obtain immeasurable merit-and-fortune." And below "one should generate a pure mind" it further says: "One should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma." Hence the elder now says, "then true reality is born; one should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rare merit and virtue," which likewise corresponds exactly to the text above. The elder takes it that the reason the World-Honored One says one should not grasp marks and should generate the pure mind is that one must be far apart from the false marks of the senses, objects, and consciousness before one can give rise to the true reality of the pure mind. What is called obtaining immeasurable merit-and-fortune is because one accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma. "Most supreme, foremost, and rare" only a Buddha can be called; below it is affixed the one word "Dharma," and above it further says "one should know." Both guard against misunderstanding and tell one: one should know that this person who generates the pure mind, though not yet a Buddha, has already accomplished the Dharma of becoming a Buddha. What is that Dharma? It is what is called being apart from the false marks of the senses, objects, and consciousness and giving rise to the true reality of the pure mind. One should know that such a person, through true faith, can leave the false and reveal the true, responding in a single thought, and his merit and virtue have already accomplished the foremost and rare bodhisattva. Reaching this position, he has already transcended the ordinary and entered the sage, and only now is Buddhahood possible. For one must first become a bodhisattva before one can become a Buddha. (The "one should know" here corresponds exactly to the "one should know" in the text above.) Hence one must accomplish the foremost and rare merit and virtue before one accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma. Is this not where the elder's deep understanding of the meaning returns? And knowing that when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born and accomplishment attained is not this the direction of the elder's deep understanding of the meaning?

From the meaning and purport the elder understood above, we too may awaken to this: since to realize the nature is precisely the mind of faith being pure, then the reason we must open understanding is nothing else than to make faith grow bright. And the reason we must advance in practice is nothing else than to make faith grow. For faith is the trunk, and understanding, practice, and realization are its helpers. From this one can further awaken to the fact that faith is the trunk; hence it is said that faith is the gate of entry to the path, and that faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit and virtue. Hence a student of Buddhism must first of all possess faith. And this whole sutra makes its meaning and purport clear through generating faith, opening understanding, advancing in practice, and accomplishing realization. Therefore when we hear this sutra, as to how the sutra makes clear what generating faith is, what attaining understanding is, what cultivating the unsurpassed bodhi is, and what accomplishing patience is, we should first believe and enter into each one. Only then is it true faith, and only then can one open understanding and cultivate diligently and attain realization. Everywhere in the sutra the word "faith" is spoken as well; this is the place where the eye is pointed out. We should understand it thus.

There is a further meaning that must not go unknown. That faith is the trunk is intended to enable the bodhisattva who has just brought forth the mind to enter the gate. Yet one should know that one is all, and all is one. The Avataṃsaka Sutra makes this meaning clear. Hence speaking in terms of faith, understanding, practice, and realization: if faith is taken as master, then all tend toward faith; if understanding is taken as master, then all tend toward understanding. The rest follow by analogy. Hence on hearing the Dharma one should deeply grasp where its intent lies. If one clings to names and words and dies beneath the sentence, that is the great taboo in studying Buddhism, and it is not the perfectly fused and unobstructed Buddhadharma. For example, the word "faith" is indeed important, and the word "understanding" is also important. To put it plainly, among the four matters of faith, understanding, practice, and realization, not one is unimportant. And among the four words, faith and understanding are the most important, because these two matters are the most intimately connected. What is meant by most important? If a student can truly believe and deeply understand, then he can naturally cultivate diligently and attain. Otherwise how could there be any talk of cultivation and realization? Hence they are called most important. What is meant by most intimate? Understanding exists because of faith, and faith is born from understanding. The word "faith" stands first. This sutra too first speaks of generating faith and next of opening understanding. And the word "faith" penetrates to the very bottom. As said above, that understanding exists because of faith needs no saying. And the saying that faith is born from understanding is as stated before: that one can give rise to faith and take this as true already contains the sense that faith comes forth from understanding. How does faith arise? Because one takes this as true. If one has not understood the true meaning within the sutra, how could one take it as true? Further, when the elder here declares of himself the meaning and purport he has deeply understood, he opens by saying, "when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born." This likewise makes plain that without deep understanding one would not know that faith's connection is thus immense. Then faith's being born from understanding becomes all the clearer. There are many other sayings in this sutra that could be cited in proof; here I do not set them all out.

It was said above that accomplishing the foremost and rare merit and virtue is the stage of the first abode. How does one know it is the first abode? Answer: there are two points. (1) It is seen from the word "born" in the text above. (2) There is the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom as evidence. One should know that true reality appearing before one is precisely realizing the patient acceptance of non-arising. Volume fifty of the great treatise says: "In the midst of the non-arising and non-ceasing true reality of all dharmas, to believe, accept, and comprehend, unobstructed and non-retreating, is called the patient acceptance of non-arising." According to the treatise, the phrase "comprehending without obstruction and freely" is the meaning of realization. That being so, the mind of the patient acceptance of non-arising is so because it comprehends true reality. Then true reality appearing before one is precisely realizing the patient acceptance of non-arising, as can be known. And the stage of true reality appearing before one is precisely the stage of realizing the patient acceptance of non-arising, as can also be known. As for the stage of realizing the patient acceptance of non-arising, the sutras and treatises give various accounts; I have discussed this before, and here I may as well repeat it. Volume seventy-three of the great treatise says: "The bodhisattva who obtains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is called avaivartika." Avaivartika means non-retreating, which is precisely the first abode. This says that the first abode attains the patient acceptance of non-arising. The Avataṃsaka Sutra, however, says that the eighth ground realizes the patient acceptance of non-arising. The Sutras of the Humane King and the Protection of the Country place it at the seventh, eighth, and ninth grounds. These accounts differ, yet their meanings all hold. For at the first abode one attains partial realization, and from the eighth ground upward one attains the path of no further effort (that is, no more learning), and only then is it perfect. Hence to say the first abode realizes it means partial realization; to say the eighth ground and so forth realize it makes clear perfect realization. One should know that even speaking of perfect realization, if one divides it finely there are still stages. What the eighth, ninth, and tenth grounds realize is like the moon of the thirteenth night: round yet not fully round. What equal enlightenment realizes is round, yet still falls slightly short. Only at the Buddha-ground is it like the full moon of the fifteenth night, ultimately perfect. And the partial realization of the first abode is no more than the realization of one portion: it is like the moon of the first quarter, whose clear light has only just been born. Hence this sutra says "true reality is born," precisely making clear that the clear light has only just been born and one has ascended to the first abode. One should further know that the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom of the bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, in saying that the first abode attains the patient acceptance of non-arising, means the perfect-teaching first abode, not the distinct-teaching first abode. "Perfect" means that one's insight is perfectly fused; "distinct" means that one's insight, whether in principle or in practice, though exceedingly profound and refined, is nonetheless separate and distinct. Separate and distinct means not perfectly fused. One should further know that for one whose insight is perfectly fused, though his stage has only just ascended to the first abode, his insight equals that of the distinct-teaching first ground. Hence volume twelve of the Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahayana says: "Nāgārjuna says that from the first ground upward one attains the patient acceptance of non-arising." Nāgārjuna originally said the first abode, and it is said that Nāgārjuna says the first ground: this very statement makes clear that the first abode Nāgārjuna speaks of is the perfect-teaching first abode, which equals the distinct-teaching first ground. The Tiantai patriarch's Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra likewise says: "The patient acceptance of non-arising is the first ground and the first abode." Ground and abode are spoken together because what he calls the first ground refers to the distinct teaching, and what he calls the first abode speaks of the perfect teaching. From this one phrase one can see that the insight of the distinct-teaching first ground and the perfect-teaching first abode are equal. One can further see that where insight is not perfect, one must reach a ground before it is perfect. One can further see that what is called realizing one portion of the dharma-body also differs greatly. Why? One of the distinct-teaching first abode must also realize one portion of the dharma-body before he can ascend to the first abode. That being so, though he is said, like the perfect-teaching first abode, to realize one portion of the dharma-body, the size of this one portion is vastly different. Why? Because the insight of the perfect-teaching first abode equals the distinct-teaching first ground. One should know that from the first abode to the first ground there are thirty stages. Is not the one portion realized by the perfect-teaching first abode thirty times greater than the one portion realized by the distinct-teaching first abode? Therefore when one of the perfect-teaching first abode cultivates up to the first ground, though he must pass through each of the thirty stages in between, he passes through them very quickly, not with the difficulty of one of the distinct teaching. That being so, for one of the distinct teaching (that is, one whose insight is not perfect) to cultivate from the ten faiths up to the first abode must be harder than for one of the perfect teaching; this too can be understood. All these principles spoken above must not go unknown. Knowing them, one knows all the more the importance of greatly opening perfect understanding. According to the Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahayana and the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, both take the distinct-teaching first ground and the perfect-teaching first abode as realizing the patient acceptance of non-arising. Now to realize non-arising is to realize the dharma-body. The perfect-teaching first abode realizes only one portion; then the distinct-teaching first ground likewise realizes one portion, as can be known. Speaking thus, does it not follow that the distinct-teaching first abode realizes nothing at all? Yet without realizing one portion one cannot be named the first abode; how then is this meaning to be reconciled? One should know that the one portion of the distinct-teaching first ground and the perfect-teaching first abode is exceedingly bright. The distinct-teaching first abode, though it too realizes one portion, is still dim and blurred. It is like the moon of the first quarter: it appears, yet is covered by clouds. Why? Because its seeing of principle and of practice has always been separate and not fused, so that though the nature is seen it remains separated, and the realization is as though not realized. Hence only when the first ground's seeing is perfect does the name of realizing one portion become manifest. One should know it thus, and then the meaning is complete. For this reason, though the distinct-teaching first abode is said to have partial realization, it is only slightly better than resemblance. One should know that it is named resemblance because what it sees is not the true moon but the moon's reflection. It is named partial realization because what it sees is not the moon's reflection but the true moon; hence it is superior. Yet the true moon is still hidden within thick clouds; hence it falls short. Because what it sees, though true, is still blurred, its difference from the moon's reflection is very slight. This is why it is superior, and yet said to fall short. Yet although the difference is very slight, in the one case what is seen, though exceedingly bright, is a moon in water, glimpsed indirectly from the opposite side; hence it is called resemblance. In the other case what is seen, though exceedingly blurred, is the true moon, directly contemplated from the heaven of the nature; hence though it falls short, it is still superior. One should know it thus, and only then is the meaning thorough.
(Chou) 2. Making clear true reality.
["World-Honored One, what is called true reality is precisely non-mark; therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality."]

This section explains what true reality is and why it is named true reality. "What is called true reality" is like saying "this so-called true reality." "Is precisely non-mark" means one must not misunderstand it as speaking of a mark. Since it is named true reality and yet called non-mark, this precisely makes clear that what is spoken of is the nature. "Tathagata" is a name for the virtue of the nature. "The Tathagata speaks" means speaking in terms of the nature. "Named" is a provisional name. Since it is non-mark, why is it named true reality? Hence he further explains: precisely because it is non-mark, therefore, speaking in terms of the nature, it is provisionally named true reality. The meaning is that the nature differs from the falseness of marks, and so it is named true reality.

The meaning of the sutra text is inexhaustible, so I can only explain it layer by layer. Here I first give the one meaning as above, so that the general purport may be understood. If one explained it only thus, it would not be thorough. One may ask: the nature is fundamentally not marks; why then is it provisionally named true reality? This meaning must be explained in four layers.

(1) The word "true" has two meanings: one is the meaning of solidity, the other is the meaning of reality. "Solidity" means being obstructive and solid. For example, if a cup is filled full with something and is very hard and compact, then it has substance and obstruction. Why? Because it can no longer receive anything else; this is what is meant by solidity. Yet the nature-body is empty and numinous, precisely the opposite of solidity. Being empty, it is not solid; being numinous, it is not obstructive. Hence one knows that the "true" of true reality is not the meaning of solidity but the meaning of reality. "Reality" makes clear that it is not false. "False" also has two meanings. First, "false" means empty and "delusive" means erroneous. Second, "false" means unreal and "delusive" means illusory. The first meaning is that it is nothing and is bad. The second meaning is not only not bad, but not nothing either; it is the meaning of unreal existence and illusory marks. It was said above: "All marks whatsoever are false." What is called false is the second meaning, not the first. This meaning stands precisely opposed to the meaning of reality. That being so, marks are false and the nature is real: plainly these are opposites, and the nature is plainly not marks. Why then is it also named "mark"? One should know that in the Buddhist scriptures not a single word or name is without skillful means. What is skillful means? It is the ability to enable one, by means of this name and word, to pass from this side to that side without clinging to one side. One should know that precisely because the nature is fundamentally not marks, and yet can manifest all marks, being empty yet not empty, this is why the nature is real. The sutra line "therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality" precisely reveals this meaning. "Therefore" carries on from the non-mark above. "Tathagata" refers to the nature. That non-mark is the nature and is named true reality is because, speaking in terms of the nature, it is named true, making clear the meaning that the nature is not false but is real. And again, speaking in terms of the nature, it is named mark, making clear the meaning that the nature, though not marks, can manifest marks. Moreover, from this sutra text one can see that even this name "true reality" can enable one to understand the meaning that the nature-body is absolutely unconditioned. For the doctrine that nature and marks are opposed is only so when viewed on the surface. If one examines the actual fact and looks deeply, apart from the Tathagata's nature-body there is no mark to speak of, and one can know that the nature-body is absolutely unconditioned. The sutra line "the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality" is like saying, "as spoken by the Tathagata, it is named true reality." This precisely reveals the meaning that without the nature one cannot speak of the real, and without the nature one cannot manifest marks. This is the first reason why the nature is provisionally named true reality.

(2) The meaning of this section and the earlier meaning that "if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata" illuminate each other. For the earlier text made clear: if one sees only the side of marks, one leans toward existence; if one sees only the side of non-marks, one leans toward emptiness. Neither can see the Tathagata's nature. Why? Because the nature is emptiness and existence simultaneously and together present. Does the Awakening of Faith not make clear that the Tathagata-garbha is complete with the meaning of emptiness and non-emptiness? Is this not emptiness and existence at once? Hence one must be able to see that marks are precisely non-marks before one sees the Tathagata. One should know that one should see marks as non-marks, and also see non-marks as marks. Marks as non-marks: form is precisely emptiness. Non-marks as marks: emptiness is precisely form. The earlier text already made clear the meaning that form is precisely emptiness; here it further makes clear the meaning that emptiness is precisely form, so that, joining earlier and later and viewing them together, one may understand all the better the meaning that emptiness and existence are simultaneously and together present. The sutra text first says, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark," making clear that marks are precisely non-marks. It then says, "therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality": "therefore" carries on from the non-mark above, and continues with "speaks of it as named true reality," making clear that non-marks are marks. Marks being precisely non-marks and non-marks being marks is precisely the true meaning of the Tathagata-garbha; hence it says "the Tathagata speaks." Hence it first says, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark" (with stress on "true"), and afterwards says, "speaks of it as named true reality" (with stress on "true"). This is the second reason why the nature is provisionally named true reality. The earlier text, in saying that seeing marks is precisely non-marks, already contained the meaning that non-marks are marks, but did not state it plainly. Hence here, by making clear what true reality is, it plainly states and reveals it to supply what was lacking. It first speaks of marks being precisely non-marks and afterwards of non-marks being marks, precisely making clear that it carries on from marks being precisely non-marks and supplies what was lacking. One should further know that the two meanings, marks being precisely non-marks and non-marks being marks, originally include each other and are together present; hence after saying that marks are precisely non-marks it uses the two characters "therefore" to carry on and state it, both to make clear that it supplies the earlier meaning and to make clear that the two meanings are originally linked throughout.

(3) The Buddhist scriptures often say that the nature-body is empty and quiescent. Because this guards against people misunderstanding the emptiness of the nature-body as nothingness and its quiescence as dead quiescence, the nature-body is further named true reality. "True" means that it truly exists and is not nothingness. "Reality" means that it blazes forth and appears, and is not dead quiescence. Here the text precisely makes this meaning clear. The two characters "non-mark" speak of its emptiness and quiescence. Why? If all marks are non-marks, is this not empty and quiescent? Yet one fails to see that precisely because all marks are non-marks, therefore, in terms of the Tathagata's nature-body, it is spoken of as named true reality. To name it "true" reveals that it is wondrously still and all-holding, constant and unchanging; though empty, it is not nothing. To name it "reality" reveals that whatever comes it shows itself, the barbarian comes and it appears, the Chinese comes and it appears; though quiescent, it constantly illumines. This is the third reason why the nature is named true reality.

(4) The ancient worthies explained the meaning of true reality as "no marks and yet not without marks." This explanation is most wondrous and extremely concise and clear. "No marks and yet not without marks" should be explained under two meanings to be complete. First: the nature-body is fundamentally not marks, hence it is said to be without marks. Yet though it is not marks, all marks arise in dependence on the nature; hence it is further said to be not without marks. Second: though it can manifest all marks, it still has nothing to do with any mark; hence it is said to be without marks, which makes clear that it is precisely marks and yet apart from marks. The nature is indeed not marks, yet it does not itself give rise to a single thought saying "I am not marks"; hence it is said to be not without marks, which makes clear that it is precisely non-marks and yet apart from non-marks. The second meaning is deeper than the first; in sum, it makes clear that the nature-body is apart from thought. Without thought there is no such thing as marks or non-marks; hence when thought is apart, marks and non-marks are all apart. That being so, because the nature-body is without marks, though one names it "mark," it still has nothing to do with that. And because the nature-body is not without marks, to name it "mark" is no harm to it at all. Moreover, "mark" has two meanings. One means outer mark, that is, the sense of an object-mark. The other means mark-form, which is a term of analogy. To name the nature as mark certainly cannot be taken rigidly as an object-mark. Hence the phrase "true reality" is like saying "true mark-form." "No marks and yet not without marks" is precisely the true mark-form of the nature-body; hence it is named true reality. Explained thus, the meaning of "no marks and yet not without marks" is indeed complete. And explained thus, the explanation of true reality is also quite skillful. And this phrase, "no marks and yet not without marks," the ancient worthies originally grasped from the sutra text of this section. Hence as "no marks and yet not without marks" possesses the two meanings stated above, so the sutra text of this section also possesses these two meanings.

Speaking in terms of the first meaning: because the nature-body is fundamentally not marks, the sutra text says, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark." Yet though it is not marks, all marks arise in dependence on the nature; hence the sutra text says, "therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality."

Speaking in terms of the second meaning: because marks and non-marks are all apart, the sutra text says, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark." "Non" carries the sense of being apart. True reality is precisely non-mark: is this not marks and non-marks both apart? Marks and non-marks both apart: such is the true mark-form of the Tathagata-garbha, exactly so. Hence the sutra text states it further: because marks and non-marks are both apart, speaking in terms of the Tathagata's nature-body, it may be named the true mark-form. This is the fourth reason why the nature is named true reality.

The Buddha speaks of the original nature and applies various names to it; and of all dharmas too he invariably uses every kind of expression and sets up every kind of term. This meaning is most essential, and no one has ever spoken of it; now I will briefly explain it for you all.

One should know that the Buddha's speaking of the Dharma is originally to break the clinging of sentient beings. Because of partiality and selfishness they cling, and because of clinging they grow more partial and selfish. The reason sentient beings create karma and suffer, transmigrating without end and dying and being born without rest, lies entirely in this. And the reason the world has so much affliction, so much contention, even to the point of slaughter filling the cities and slaughter filling the fields, is in every case none other than this. The World-Honored One came forth to save the world and deliver it from suffering, and so he must first break this. One should know that the reason sentient beings are partial and selfish and form clingings is nothing else: their wisdom is short and shallow. Seeing only one side of every matter, they take all dharmas to be fixed, and what they themselves see as necessarily unchangeable. They do not know that they are partial, and do not know that they are clinging. Hence the Buddha gives them a needle at the crown of the head, saying, "There is no fixed dharma," to break the root of their disease of partial clinging. And in speaking any one dharma he invariably uses every kind of expression and sets up every kind of term, precisely to show that dharmas have nothing fixed. This word "dharma" is used in a broad sense, taking in worldly and world-transcending dharmas alike. If one takes it that only world-transcending dharmas are so, one contradicts the Buddha's intent.

One should further know that the essential reason a person studies Buddhism, and the essential reason a student of Buddhism cultivates contemplation, is nothing else. By contemplating the perfectly fused Buddhist principle, one can transform all one's former conceptions and dissolve the disease of partial clinging. Hence one who studies Buddhism without cultivating contemplation gains very little. Why? Because only by cultivating contemplation can one understand the principle. Because contemplation is deep, afterwards the understanding of principle is deep. Because contemplation is perfect, afterwards the understanding of principle is perfect. And conversely, when the understanding of principle is deep, contemplation grows deeper; when the understanding of principle is perfect, contemplation grows more perfect. Thus cultivating and practicing back and forth, wisdom increases in brightness back and forth. Already without knowing or perceiving it, the clinging mind gradually dissolves and deluded thoughts quietly cease. Hence the wondrous function of what is called dismissing clinging lies here; it is not a forced dismissal. And the wondrous function of what is called cutting off thought likewise lies here; it is not a forced cutting off.

That being so, where exactly is this "here"? One should know that the Buddha, in speaking the Dharma, never states a single sentence flatly, never states a single word flatly. And whenever he speaks one dharma he invariably uses every kind of expression and sets up every kind of term, for no other reason than to make those who hear the Dharma view it from every side, and only then understand the meaning and purport within it. This is precisely where the wondrous function lies. Why? Because by this means one has already broken the bad habit of looking always at one side and clinging partially. And what this sutra speaks is all the more perfect and all the more wondrous; it is truly the diamond sword of wisdom. Why? Because if one can truly pass from viewing every side to deep contemplation and perfect contemplation, there is no delusion it does not break. Moreover, since one must view from every side before understanding the meaning and purport, one naturally cannot but read the Great Vehicle widely, to broaden one's hearing and seeing. And one further cannot but quietly illumine with awareness, to grasp its refinement and subtlety. Concentration and wisdom are thereby present. If one can truly be thus, then not only does one gain freedom and benefit in every kind of practice; in all worldly dharmas one can advance and withdraw with ease. And the turning from ordinary to sage has already laid its foundation here. Why? Because concentration and wisdom increase daily and deluded thoughts decrease daily. This is the essential key to hearing the Dharma, the most wondrous secret for entering Buddhism; one should urgently fix one's eyes on it.

I myself respectfully take this intent as my foundation, and whenever I explain one meaning I invariably give various explanations, turning it over and around with care, never wearying of detail, for no other reason than the hope that those who hear may open their minds and hearts and gain more means of contemplation. For the original face fundamentally cannot be reached by words and speech, and sentient beings have long since forgotten it. If, amid what cannot be spoken, one does not set up many skillful means to speak of it, how can one cultivate contemplation? What precedes makes clear the great benefit of viewing from every side, of deep contemplation, and of perfect contemplation. If one does the opposite, the harm is also very great. Take, for example, the two words "faith" and "understanding." One often sees people who insist one-sidedly that it is enough simply to muster faith and recite the Buddha's name honestly, and who forbid the reading and reciting of all scriptures, shelving the treasures of the Great Vehicle still higher. If someone studies the teaching and delights in attending Dharma assemblies, they scold him as not honest. One should know that honest Buddha-recitation requires a certain level. If one has not understood the slightest bit of the meaning and purport of Buddha-recitation, how can one be honest? To insist too far in this way not only dulls students but also contradicts the Buddha's intent. For the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations plainly says that one who seeks rebirth in the Pure Land should read and recite the Great Vehicle and understand the supreme meaning. At the very least one must hear the supreme meaning and not be alarmed at heart. Hence of those who study by such methods, either they cannot rouse themselves and give up halfway, or they walk into a side path without knowing it. This is the fault of not knowing that faith is born from understanding. One also sees people who never let a scroll out of their hands, broadly learned and widely informed, who read through the entire canon more than once, yet never once burn a stick of incense or make a single bow, and do not know to revere the Three Treasures. Of the layer of practice there is no need to speak. Even their rolling speech and surging writing are plausible yet false, harming the Dharma and harming others. This again is the fault of not knowing that understanding comes forth from faith. This was why I did not shrink from tedious words before.

It was said above that the World-Honored One in speaking the Dharma never states a single word flatly, and so forth. One should know that the Buddha does not do this on purpose; it is because his wisdom is perfect and all-pervading, and his words and utterances are naturally so. Not only the Buddha is so; bodhisattvas are so too, and great virtuous patriarchs are all so. Hence with regard to all sutras and treatises and all the words of the ancient worthies, even in the most trivial place, one must not read carelessly. Not to read carelessly means one should view each one from every side and understand it deeply. One should further know that the insight of Buddhas and bodhisattvas is far beyond what we ordinary beings can hope to see. Even if one can understand deeply, it is no more than seeing one part in ten million. Even if one can speak well, it is no more than speaking one part in ten million. Though one spoke for a whole kalpa, one could not speak it out. For example, the meaning of "one should know" in the section above has already been explained in three or four layers. Yet it still contains many meanings. Now I may as well speak of several more, to show that it cannot be spoken out.

(1) One should know that this sutra must be heard. Why? Because such a person's generation of true faith and accomplishment of merit and virtue comes from hearing this sutra. Moreover, that this sutra must be heard means, in other words, that prajñā must be studied.

(2) One should know that faith is most essential. Why? Because the birth of true reality comes from the purity of the mind of faith. From this one can know that the earlier words, that keeping the precepts and cultivating merit can, with regard to such words and chapter-and-verse, give rise to faith and take this as true, deserve to be pondered three times over. In plain terms: if one wishes to study prajñā, one should give rise to true faith. If one wishes to give rise to true faith, one should first keep the precepts and cultivate merit.

(3) One should know that to turn from ordinary to sage and not retreat from bodhi, one must be apart from marks and see the nature. The line about accomplishment makes clear that one ascends to the first abode and transcends the ordinary to enter the sage. To be called one who abides makes clear that on reaching this position the bodhi mind can no longer retreat. This is the accomplishment of faith. And the mind being pure makes clear being apart from marks. True reality being born makes clear seeing the nature. This is why it first says that one should know prajñā must be studied. Why? Because without studying prajñā one cannot be apart from marks and see the nature. This is why it next says that one should know one must first keep the precepts and cultivate merit. Why? Because without keeping the precepts and cultivating merit there is no true faith. And without true faith one cannot have a pure mind of faith. These are all things a student should urgently follow and practice. Without practicing thus one cannot accomplish; hence it says "one should know." "One should know" makes clear that this must not go unknown.

Further, to extend the point: from the meaning of the section expressing praise and rejoicing, if one does not bring forth the great mind and does not hear this sutra, then at the very best one can only open the wisdom-eye and become an arhat of the fourth fruit. From the meaning of the section making clear the accomplishment, if one does hear this sutra and the mind of faith is pure, then at the very least one can give birth to true reality and become a bodhisattva of the first abode. This too is something students should know. Speaking thus, one can see that the sutra's meaning is truly inexhaustible and truly cannot be spoken out. One can see that in hearing the Dharma one must view from every side. For example, when I explain true reality through various meanings, if a hearer takes it only as an explanation of why the original nature is named true reality, that is not my intent in explaining it over and over in detail. And if one understands only why the nature is named true reality, that too brings the hearer no great benefit. Why? True reality is the original face of the master within us all. Such a true face fundamentally can only be known through realization. That being so, how is it to be realized? Nothing else: one must only apply effort in reflecting back. Not only should one reflect back while hearing; one should further, in the still of night and at the break of dawn, and when meeting objects and following conditions, rely on the various meanings spoken here and contemplate them deeply. One may take up one meaning alone, or merge all the meanings together; either is acceptable. In the still of night and at the break of dawn, one contemplates within one's own mind; when meeting objects and following conditions, one contemplates upon all dharmas. If one can truly be thus, the benefit is boundless. One should know that the reason the Buddha sets up various names for the original nature is to make it easy for people to grasp the body through the name. And among the various names, the one name "true reality" makes it comparatively easy to understand not clinging to the two extremes and the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. This is also the reason the elder singled out this name to speak of. And the reason I in turn open up various meanings from this name and explain them is to make it easy for the hearer, when reflecting back and applying effort, to have more means of understanding, not merely to explain the meaning of the name. From this one can know the significance of opening up various meanings to explain it.

This section has a further essential meaning. For the elder's speaking here is indeed to explain what true reality is and why it is named true reality, and so forth; but it is in fact also to indicate the method of applying effort. How is this known? Since here it makes clear that marks and non-marks are both apart, it corresponds exactly to what the text below says, that being apart from all marks one is called a Buddha. The word "apart" involves great work; without work, how could one be apart? How could one be called a Buddha? Hence one knows that here the text contains the work of cultivation. One should know that to speak the one word "non" is to cut off the hundred negations. It is also to be apart from all four propositions. That is, existence is also apart, non-existence is also apart, both existence and non-existence are also apart, neither existence nor non-existence are also apart. From this one can know that when the ancient worthies explained true reality as "no marks and yet not without marks," this one word "no" is likewise the no that is absolutely unconditioned, not the no spoken in contrast to yes. For marks and non-marks are fundamentally terms of opposition. Where there is opposition, there is change. Where there is change, there is arising and ceasing. Where there is arising and ceasing, there is no firmness. But the nature-body is truly constant through all ages, ultimately firm. Being firm, it has no arising and ceasing. Without arising and ceasing, there is no change. Without change, there is no opposition. Without opposition, it is absolutely unconditioned. Absolutely unconditioned means that though marks and non-marks never depart from mind and nature, mind and nature nonetheless stand utterly beyond marks and non-marks. In plain terms: marks are existence, and non-marks are non-existence. To stand beyond these, is that not to stand beyond existence and non-existence? Then the saying "no marks and yet not without marks" is speaking of absolute nothingness and not of a nothingness spoken in contrast to something: this can be understood at a glance. That being so, how can one attain absolute nothingness? By being apart from all four propositions of existence and non-existence. Hence the sutra text says, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark." To speak the one word "non" is to indicate the work of cultivation. It is to cause the student who wishes to see true reality to quiet the mind and understand on the ground that all is non. If one understands that true reality is precisely non-mark, one understands that if the mind holds the slightest shadow of marks or non-marks, it is not true reality. Hence the line "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark" is exceedingly sharp; it cannot be touched even lightly, for whoever touches it loses the life of wisdom. In plain terms, it causes the student to enter at the tip of a single hair.

Now, wishing you all to have a place to set your hands, I will further, in accordance with this principle, speak one skillful means. What is that means? One must contemplate with precision before a single thought has been stirred. If a thought arises and leans toward existence, one scolds it, saying "non." Or if it leans toward non-existence, one likewise scolds it, saying "non." And even thoughts of both existence and non-existence, and thoughts of neither existence nor non-existence, are all dismissed with the word "non" as the scolding. This is the most wondrous gate of contemplation. One should know that if a thought does not arise, well and good; but if it arises, it must cling to one of the four propositions. To negate them all here is the sharp blade and keen axe that is apart from thought. Is this not the most wondrous gate of contemplation? As for the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices of world-transcending dharmas, one should advance diligently in each according to the Dharma, yet never let the slightest knot form in the breast. Advancing diligently in each is non-destruction, which is "not without marks." And the mind being as though nothing were happening is non-clinging, which is "without marks." As for all worldly dharmas, when a matter comes one responds, and when the matter has passed one lets it rest. Though one responds, one can let it rest; though one lets it rest, one can respond. This is what is meant by being able to pick it up and put it down. Whether in worldly or world-transcending dharmas, wherever one leans even slightly, one dismisses it with the word "non." Pondering the meaning and purport of being apart from all four propositions over a long time and practicing thus, one can reach the point where the time of response is the time of rest, and the time of rest is the time of response. Naturally one does not cling to the two extremes and accords with the middle way, and marks and non-marks, existence and non-existence, all four propositions, are all apart. This again is the most wondrous gate of practice.

The sutra plainly says, "Therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality." This shows the student that the reason he negates and yet still speaks is merely to make clear that there is no need to destroy. One should know that though it is spoken, it is a provisional name; the Tathagata's nature-body must still be self-realized apart from names and words. And being apart from names and words is being apart from thought. And of the skillful means for being apart from thought, none surpasses contemplating before a single thought has been stirred. If a single thought arises, one negates everything and drives it out: is this not precisely indicating the work of cultivation? One should know that from the section above, "when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born," to here, this is precisely the elder's deep understanding of the meaning and purport. Hence one who hears the sutra should understand it deeply thus.

The World-Honored One sets up various names for the original nature, and the elder further singles out the one name true reality to speak of, both to make it easy for students to recognize the original nature. Hence the meaning of true reality should be developed at length. The great treatise states four lines of verse on true reality, the most refined and detailed, and most worth knowing, so that one may constantly illumine with awareness. True reality is the original face of the nature. Precisely because the original nature is obscured do beings become sentient beings. Now if one wishes to turn from ordinary to sage, can one do so without truly and vividly recognizing it? The verse says: "All is real, all is unreal, and all is real and also unreal; all is unreal and not unreal: this is named the true reality of all dharmas." From this one can see the bodhisattva's skill in speaking the Dharma. He does not speak in terms of the word "mark" but in terms of the word "real": this is the first point. He does not speak in terms of the nature but in terms of all dharmas: this is the second point. One should know that to speak of "mark" is a provisional name, merely to enable people to understand the condition of the original nature. Hence not speaking in terms of marks points out that the word "mark" should not be taken rigidly. If it is taken rigidly, one has already clung to marks. That he speaks in terms of the word "real" also has deep intent. For people cling to marks because they mistakenly take them as real. If one knows that all dharmas are real and also unreal, unreal and yet real, then one knows that all dharma-marks are precisely non-marks, and non-marks are precisely marks. Is such speaking not skillful?

That he speaks in terms of all dharmas must be made clear under three meanings. (1) It lets one know that outside the mind there are no dharmas. The Buddha says that all dharmas are merely illusory marks without real substance. The substance is only the pure mind. Hence it is said that the ten thousand dharmas are mind only. It is also said that outside the mind there are no dharmas. Hence one can make clear true reality through all dharmas, because the true reality of all dharmas is the nature. To speak in terms of dharmas is no different from speaking in terms of the nature. (2) It makes it easy for people to understand. Sentient beings have long since forgotten the original nature, while all dharmas are known and seen in common by sentient beings. It is better to speak in terms of all dharmas, so that through all dharmas one may awaken to the mind-nature. (3) It makes clear the one true dharma-realm. The Awakening of Faith says: "Because they do not know the one dharma-realm, unawakened thought arises, and there is ignorance." Thus they become sentient beings. The one dharma-realm is the one true dharma-realm. The ten dharma-realms with their myriad teeming forms, and true suchness, are one. This is the meaning that all is of one substance. If one knows that the true condition of all dharmas is in every case the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, then from the ten directions' Buddhas above down to all sentient beings below, and mountains, rivers, and the great earth, sentient and insentient, all without exception take the pure mind as their substance, as can be clearly known. Because the true reality of the pure mind is fundamentally the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, this is called the one true dharma-realm, also called all dharmas being one suchness. One should know that all dharmas are manifested by the mind, and since the mind-nature is the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, all dharmas are without exception the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. This is the second point of his skill.

Nāgārjuna took Aśvaghoṣa as his teacher; hence the Awakening of Faith already makes clear true suchness through all dharmas. Truly the robe and bowl have been passed down. "All is real": all dharmas plainly stand before the eyes. These words break the clinging to nothingness. "All is unreal": all dharmas in their very substance are empty. These words break the clinging to existence. And further, to guard against people hearing this and clinging to "both existent and non-existent" or "neither existent nor non-existent," he speaks the next two lines. "And" carries the sense of joining: it means one must not look only at the first line, but must join it with the second and third lines and understand them together. The meaning is as if to say: what has just been said, that all dharmas are real and unreal, is not separate and unfused. One should know that it is precisely real and yet unreal, unreal and yet not unreal. Real and yet unreal is what is called existence and yet non-existence, form and yet emptiness. Unreal and yet not unreal is what is called non-existent and yet existing, emptiness and yet form. In this way all four propositions are dismissed, and such is the true condition of all dharmas. It is also such as the true condition of the nature-body. And he concludes: this is named the true reality of all dharmas.

He further makes clear that the dharma-nature fundamentally cannot be spoken. To speak of it as true reality is likewise a provisional name and one must not cling to it. People often hear that all four propositions are dismissed and that emptiness and existence are simultaneous, and cannot help doubting. They think that "both existent and non-existent" and "neither existent nor non-existent" are no different in meaning from the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. Why? To speak of the simultaneity of emptiness and existence: does it not make clear that to say existent is acceptable and to say non-existent is acceptable? And does it not further make clear that to say only existent is wrong and to say only non-existent is wrong? That being so, why is it that to say "both existent and non-existent" or to say "neither existent nor non-existent" is called partial clinging and dismissed? To speak thus is an error, a great error! For such a person has not understood the meaning of the words "both existent and non-existent" and "neither existent nor non-existent," nor has he understood the meaning of the words "the simultaneity of emptiness and existence." One should know that the two lines "both existent and non-existent" and "neither existent nor non-existent" carry on from the lines of existence and non-existence above them, and hence are called the four propositions.

The intent of one who says "both existent and non-existent" is this: he thinks that the first person says only existent and the second says only non-existent, each leaning to one side, and this is indeed a fault. I, however, am not like that. I say that all dharmas are both existent and non-existent. Since both extremes are affirmed, the fault of leaning to one extreme is removed. He fails to see that if one says existent one cannot say non-existent, and if one says non-existent one cannot say existent; yet to say "both existent and non-existent" contradicts one's own words. Moreover, he takes it that existent is also right and non-existent is also right. Since the words are ambiguous and take either side, and the meaning is separate and unfused, it should be dismissed.

The intent of one who says "neither existent nor non-existent" is this: he thinks that what the third person says is indeed faulty, and that I differ from him. I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent. Since both extremes are alike dismissed, the fault of the third person's clinging to the two extremes is removed. He fails to see that "neither existent" is precisely non-existent, so why further say "nor non-existent"? And "nor non-existent" is precisely existent, so why further say "neither existent"? Is this not idle disputation? Moreover, he still takes it that existent is existent and non-existent is non-existent. His separateness and lack of fusion is likewise the same fault as the third person's. Hence it should be dismissed. Further, the insight of the third person, having said that existence and non-existence are both affirmed, still leans to the side of existence. And the insight of the fourth person, saying that existence and non-existence are both negated, still leans to the side of emptiness. Should these not be dismissed? (Both-affirmed resembles both-illumined, and both-negated resembles both-concealed. Yet in fact they are greatly different. For the words both-illumined and both-concealed make clear that one has attained the middle; whereas the doctrines of both-affirmed and both-negated know only the two extremes.) As for the meaning of the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, it makes clear that when it is empty it is precisely when it is existent, and when it is existent one sees the time of emptiness. Emptiness and existence perfectly fused, since they are not two, are without extremes. When extremes are not even present, where could one cling? Compared with both existent and non-existent and neither existent nor non-existent, the difference in meaning is as heaven from an abyss: how can one say there is no difference!
